text:
Good Friday evening from a small Texas town. 🌅

Numbers 6:26 (NIV)

“The LORD turn his face toward you and give you peace.”🙏

There's something special about Friday evenings.

The workweek is coming to an end, the sun is settling over the horizon, and for a little while, the world seems to slow down.

Maybe this week has been wonderful. Maybe it's been exhausting. Or maybe it's been one of those weeks when you've simply done your best to get through each day.

Whatever kind of week you've had, I hope you'll take a moment tonight to appreciate the beautiful blessing found in this Scripture.

“The LORD turn his face toward you and give you peace.”

What a comforting thought. The Creator of heaven and earth cares about us personally. He sees our struggles, hears our prayers, and knows the burdens we carry, even when we haven't spoken a word about them.

And the peace He offers isn't dependent on everything in our lives going perfectly.

It's the kind of peace that can steady our hearts when circumstances are uncertain. The kind that reminds us we're loved when we feel overlooked. The kind that helps us find rest even when tomorrow still holds unanswered questions.

Sometimes we spend so much time thinking about what went wrong during the week that we forget to recognize what went right.

The prayers that were answered. The unexpected kindness. The little moments of laughter. The strength we found when we weren't sure we had any left.

And even on the difficult days, God was there.

Tonight, we don't have to carry every worry into the weekend. We can be grateful for what we've accomplished, forgive ourselves for what remains unfinished, and trust God with the things beyond our control.

Let's pray: 🙏

Heavenly Father, thank You for bringing us safely through another week.

Thank You for the blessings we've received, the challenges You've helped us overcome, and the quiet ways You've reminded us of Your love.

Lord, as this Friday evening settles around us, we ask for Your peace to fill our hearts and homes.

For those who are weary, provide rest. For those who are struggling with illness, bring healing and comfort. For those carrying grief, loneliness, or worry, wrap them in Your loving presence.

Help us release the frustrations of the past week and welcome the weekend with grateful hearts.

Watch over our families and loved ones. Guide those who are traveling, protect those who are working tonight, and bring comfort to anyone who feels alone.

May Your face shine upon us, Your grace sustain us, and Your peace remain with us through the night.

In Jesus' name, Amen. 🙏

As the sun sets on another Friday, remember that you don't have to have a perfect life to experience God's perfect peace.

Sometimes the greatest blessing is simply knowing that whatever tomorrow brings, we are never beyond His love and care.

Peace and grace to you. 
Rest well tonight. 
See you in the morning for coffee. ☕

text:
On September 4, 1991, Kenny Rogers stood at Dottie West’s bedside at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville.

Five days earlier, the 58-year-old country star had been critically injured in a car crash on her way to the Grand Ole Opry. 

Her car had broken down, so an elderly neighbor offered her a ride. He lost control exiting the highway, and the car struck an embankment. West suffered a ruptured spleen and severe liver damage. Two surgeries failed to stop the bleeding.

Rogers, her longtime duet partner, flew in to see her. He took her hand and promised that if she pulled through, they would go back into the studio and record one more song together. 

Contemporary reports note that he spoke to her even though she was largely unresponsive, hoping she could hear him. 

One account says she whispered “Thank you.”
She never made it out of the operating room. During her third surgery that morning, her heart failed and she died on the table.

The promised duet was never recorded. Rogers later said of her: “What made Dottie unique is that when she sang about pain, she felt pain. 

When she sang about love, she felt love. And when she sang about beauty, she felt that beauty. While some performers sang words, she sang emotions.”

Their partnership had already given country music some of its most memorable duets. 

That final quiet moment in a Nashville hospital room was the last one they would share. 🌹

text:
▫️🌿 Rhode Island Approves Cannabis Home Delivery Until 11 PM, Expanding Marijuana Access▫️

• 🕚 Extended Delivery Hours: Rhode Island's Cannabis Control Commission voted 2 to 1 to expand legal marijuana delivery hours from the previous 8 AM to 8 PM schedule to a new window of 7 AM to 11 PM. The decision allows authorized dispensaries to serve customers later into the evening.

• 🚗 Marijuana Delivered to Doorsteps: Licensed cannabis retailers with approved delivery plans can transport marijuana products directly to residential addresses. Customers no longer need to visit a physical dispensary for every purchase.

• 🪪 Strict Age Verification: Recreational cannabis deliveries are restricted to adults aged 21 and older. Customers must present valid identification, and the recipient's name must match the original order. Registered medical marijuana patients are subject to separate eligibility requirements.

• 💰 Business Expansion Opportunities: Longer delivery hours could generate additional revenue for dispensaries, increase evening sales and create more opportunities for delivery workers. However, individual businesses must decide whether to expand their operating schedules.

• ⚠️ Safety Concerns Spark Debate: Commissioner Robert Jacquard opposed the expansion, warning that nighttime marijuana deliveries could increase risks of robbery or violence. Supporters argued that extended hours would improve convenience and potentially reduce impaired driving.

• 🏛️ Regulators Respond to Industry Demand: Commission Chair Michelle Reddish said cannabis businesses had submitted multiple requests seeking expanded delivery hours. The approval reflects growing interest in making regulated marijuana sales more accessible.

• 📈 Broader Cannabis Industry Implications: Rhode Island's decision illustrates how states with legalized recreational marijuana are expanding retail services beyond traditional storefronts. The policy could encourage more dispensaries to develop home delivery operations, although the actual economic impact remains uncertain.

• 📋 Implementation Still Matters: The commission has approved the expanded hours, but that does not mean every dispensary immediately offers delivery until 11 PM. Businesses must maintain the necessary authorization and update their operations before providing extended service.

▫️🛒 Instacart Explores Potential $17 Billion Sale to DoorDash or Uber as Grocery Delivery Industry Faces Major Consolidation▫️

• 🏢 Instacart Considering a Major Takeover: Grocery delivery giant Instacart is exploring a potential sale after holding preliminary discussions with DoorDash and Uber. The company has reportedly enlisted an investment bank to evaluate strategic options, potentially ending its 14 years as an independent business.

• 💰 Potential Acquisition Worth $16 Billion to $17 Billion: Instacart currently carries a market valuation of approximately $12 billion. A takeover premium of 30% to 40% could push a potential acquisition price to between $16 billion and $17 billion, although no formal offer has been announced.

• 📈 Instacart Shares Surge on Takeover Speculation: Instacart shares jumped approximately 9% following reports of the discussions. Meanwhile, Uber shares declined nearly 3%, and DoorDash dropped more than 4%, reflecting investor concerns about the financial implications of a major acquisition.

• 🤝 Uber Discussions Reportedly Ended: Although Uber previously explored acquiring Instacart, subsequent reporting indicates the companies are no longer in active discussions. DoorDash remains a potential buyer, but no agreement has been reached.

• 🛍️ Grocery Delivery Competition Intensifies: Acquiring Instacart would give either company access to an established grocery marketplace, relationships with major retailers, advertising technology and delivery infrastructure. The transaction could significantly reshape competition against Amazon and traditional supermarket chains.

• 📉 Instacart's Valuation Has Fallen Dramatically: Instacart reached a private valuation of approximately $39 billion in 2021. DoorDash previously explored acquiring the company for between $40 billion and $50 billion, but those discussions collapsed partly because of regulatory concerns.

• ⚖️ Antitrust Scrutiny Could Complicate a Deal: Federal regulators could closely examine any acquisition because Uber, DoorDash and Instacart compete in grocery delivery. Combining major platforms could raise concerns about competition, delivery fees, retailer bargaining power and consumer choice.

• 📊 Instacart Remains Financially Strong Despite Slower Growth: The company reported more than $1 billion in second quarter revenue, representing 14% annual growth, alongside approximately $480 million in free cash flow. However, competition and slower growth compared with larger delivery platforms have increased pressure on its independent business model.

• 🔎 A Sale Remains Uncertain: Discussions are preliminary, and there is no guarantee that Instacart will reach an agreement with DoorDash, Uber or another potential buyer. A completed acquisition would represent one of the most significant consolidation moves in the American grocery delivery industry.

text:
▫️✈️ U.S. Airlines Choose Empty Seats Over Cheap Tickets as Rising Fuel Costs Threaten Profits▫️

✈️ Airlines Prioritize Profitability: Major U.S. airlines are increasingly willing to operate flights with empty seats rather than offer steep discounts to fill every available seat. The strategy reflects a shift toward protecting ticket prices and profitability instead of maximizing passenger volume.

⛽ Rising Fuel Costs Increase Pressure: Higher jet fuel prices are squeezing airline profit margins, making it more expensive to operate flights. Airlines are responding by maintaining stronger fares, controlling expenses, and adjusting flight schedules to reduce financial pressure.

💺 Empty Seats Become a Strategic Decision: Airlines traditionally discount unsold seats as departure approaches because even a discounted ticket can generate additional revenue. However, carriers may now prefer to preserve higher average fares rather than encourage customers to wait for last minute bargains.

📉 Airlines Restrict Flight Capacity: Instead of competing aggressively through cheaper tickets, airlines can reduce flight frequencies, eliminate weaker routes, or shift aircraft toward destinations with stronger demand. Limiting available seats can help support ticket prices while improving overall operating efficiency.

💰 Passengers Could Face Higher Airfares: Travelers hoping to secure deeply discounted tickets may encounter fewer opportunities, particularly on popular routes. Airlines maintaining pricing discipline could keep fares elevated even when some flights depart without every seat occupied.

🏢 Major Carriers Have Different Advantages: Airlines such as Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and American Airlines can benefit from premium cabins, loyalty programs, and corporate travel demand. Budget carriers face different challenges because their business models depend more heavily on attracting passengers through lower fares.

📊 The Financial Tradeoff: An empty seat generates no ticket revenue, but aggressive discounting can undermine pricing across a broader customer base. The strategy works best when airlines can maintain sufficient demand at higher fares. If demand weakens significantly, refusing to discount could ultimately hurt revenue.

🔮 Outlook for the Airline Industry: The shift suggests that airlines are increasingly emphasizing revenue per seat, capacity discipline, and sustainable margins rather than passenger growth alone. Whether the approach succeeds will depend on fuel prices, consumer spending, competition, and the willingness of travelers to continue paying higher fares.

Why selected: political leaders want deterrence without committing publicly to occupation, regime change or indefinite war.

What may actually be inside: an adversary that uses the delay to disperse missiles, improve proxy readiness and harden infrastructure.

Beneficiary: Iran gains preparation time; Washington gains only if uncertainty causes genuine Iranian restraint.

The contradiction: a conflict cannot be deliberately allowed to wither while preparations for another major campaign continue. Each message undermines the other.

BOX FOUR
THE ANTI-WAR GROUP

Selected by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan and European partners: prevent another attack through collective diplomatic signalling.

Why selected: they will absorb the energy, migration, shipping and domestic-security consequences without controlling US or Israeli decisions.

What may actually be inside: useful restraint or a public declaration lacking any enforceable offer to Iran.

Beneficiary: Gulf states gain diplomatic distance from Washington; Iran gains evidence that coalition cohesion is weakening.

Failure point: the group has not disclosed an agreed sanctions, nuclear-inspection or maritime-access sequence.

BOX FIVE
THE SAUDI MISSILE

Selected by Riyadh: develop a survivable offensive deterrent less dependent on US aircraft or vulnerable airfields.

Satellite analysis suggests that the al-Duwadimi complex could support larger solid-fuel missile motors. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the assessment. 

Why selected: Iran and the Houthis can impose costs at range while Saudi Arabia remains heavily dependent on interception.

What may actually be inside: improved deterrence or a regional missile race, proliferation concerns and pressure for still larger Iranian inventories.

Beneficiary: Saudi Arabia if capability remains credible but unused; China if technology dependence deepens; Iran if the programme justifies further expansion.

BOX SIX
RETURN TO YEMEN

Selected by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Yemen’s government: reverse Houthi territorial gains through funding, air power, advisers and selected ground forces.

Why selected: Houthi control near Bab el-Mandeb and strikes inside Saudi Arabia are no longer tolerable as a managed threat.

What may actually be inside: local gains followed by renewed attrition, coalition divisions and an expanded Houthi target list.

Beneficiary: Houthis if foreign intervention restores their resistance narrative; Saudi Arabia only if local forces hold territory without continuous external ownership.

Escalation pathway: foreign-force casualties → larger Saudi strikes → Houthi attacks on oil and airports → UAE exposure → Red Sea disruption.

BOX SEVEN.
THE WEST BANK LOCKDOWN

Selected by Israel after two soldiers were killed: immediate control, disruption and electoral demonstration of authority.

What may actually be inside: arrests and weapons seizures or collective restrictions that accelerate recruitment, undermine the Palestinian Authority and widen the confrontation.

The attackers and two Israeli soldiers were killed after a gun battle near Hebron. Israel has ordered cordons, searches and preparations for wider closure. 

Beneficiary: Netanyahu if voters reward visible strength; Hamas or Islamic Jihad if the response broadens Palestinian mobilisation.

Escalation pathway: lockdown → clashes and settler violence → militant retaliation → Gaza or Lebanon spillover.

4/7

text:
WHAT CHANGED SINCE THE PREVIOUS ASSESSMENT

CONFIRMED

President Trump said the United States might conduct another military operation against Iran and separately questioned whether to finish the conflict quickly or let it wither.

Iranian officials disclosed contingency planning against Gulf undersea cables, including attempted obstruction of repair work.

Eight European and regional foreign ministers collectively warned against renewed attacks on Iran.

Two Israeli soldiers were killed near Hebron; Israel ordered a broad security operation and preparations for a wider West Bank closure.

Brent closed at $116.72 and WTI at $103.27, their highest settlements in almost six months.

Satellite analysis indicates Saudi Arabia is expanding its al-Duwadimi solid-fuel missile-production complex.

Seven people were killed and 40 wounded in an attack on a Greek Orthodox funeral in Jordan. No group has claimed responsibility and no Iranian connection is established.

CREDIBLE BUT UNVERIFIED

A final US–Israeli decision to resume attacks after 3 November.

Iran’s account of seven tankers damaged in one night.

Iran’s assertion that it can readily access and destroy all seven named Hormuz cable systems.

Direct Russian or Chinese state provision of real-time targeting information to Iran.

Precise Saudi or Emirati Special Forces strength inside Yemen.

Iranian operational direction of European street violence.

ANALYTICAL JUDGEMENT

Iran’s cable disclosure is intended primarily to mobilise Gulf governments and US technology companies against renewed attacks.

Trump’s language increases deterrent uncertainty but also weakens allied confidence because it offers multiple incompatible war aims.

The Istanbul declaration indicates emerging diplomatic resistance to another US–Israeli campaign.

Israeli election pressure increases the probability of visible operations in the West Bank, Gaza or Lebanon, even if a direct Iran strike remains less likely before 27 October.

Saudi missile expansion reflects declining confidence that air defence and US guarantees alone can restore deterrence.

THE ACTORS AND THEIR CHOICES

IRAN AND ALIGNED ACTORS

Iran’s preferred choice remains controlled escalation below the threshold producing a unified coalition response.

Its available instruments include:

Maritime attacks, mining claims and passage intimidation.

Houthi pressure against Saudi airports, energy and government sites.

Iraqi and Lebanese proxy mobilisation.

Missiles and UAS against bases or infrastructure.

Cyber intrusion, destructive malware and data theft.

Threats against cables, cloud infrastructure and data centres.

Criminal or locally recruited facilitators overseas.

Diplomatic offers tied to sanctions relief and maritime access.

Russian and Chinese commercial, technological and diplomatic support.

Tehran believes it is selecting deterrence by expanding costs.

The box may actually contain strategic overreach. A demonstrably Iranian attack on neutral Gulf infrastructure, civilian communications or a mass-casualty target could convert reluctant regional governments into active coalition partners.

UNITED STATES

Washington can:

Continue the blockade, sanctions and commercial pressure.

Protect Hormuz traffic and Gulf infrastructure.

Conduct limited strikes against missile, drone or naval targets.

Join Israel in a broader campaign against nuclear, energy and leadership targets.

Support regional proxies and covert disruption.

Accept a negotiated sequence involving maritime access, sanctions and nuclear verification.

Allow the conflict to continue at lower intensity.

Washington believes ambiguity preserves flexibility.

The box may contain strategic incoherence. “Finish,” “wither,” “pressure” and “negotiate” are different strategies requiring different force postures and political messages. Pursuing all four simultaneously encourages Iran to prepare for the worst while conceding nothing.

2/7

text:
I think the most interesting development today is that the market seems to be increasingly ignoring the administration's diplomatic jawboning. Trump again suggested that negotiations with Iran were underway and reiterated his intention to avoid attacking before the midterms. A couple of hours later, December WTI was still trading near $103. Unlike Tuesday, when reports of a possible diplomatic agreement briefly pushed crude into the mid-$95 range, today's assurances barely seemed to interrupt the rally.

Going into this weekend, I think there's a reasonable possibility of some limited or preliminary military strikes. Israel's election is Tuesday, October 27, and we've seen considerable reporting about Netanyahu's interest in renewed operations against Iran. I don't know how that political situation will ultimately affect Israeli decisions, but I certainly wouldn't rule out an escalation before the election. At the same time, Trump is now publicly discussing the possibility of another American operation, even while maintaining that he intends to wait until after November 3.

I can also see Iran continuing to apply pressure during this period. If Washington actually intends to avoid renewed strikes until after the midterms, Tehran has a window in which it can continue imposing costs on commercial shipping and maintaining leverage in negotiations. Ansar Allah could continue doing the same against Saudi infrastructure, although I'm not convinced the Houthis are necessarily calculating their actions around the American electoral calendar in quite the same way.

I still think the underlying strategic problem is unresolved. Even if Kpler's reported recovery in regional exports is accurate, keeping those volumes moving through an ongoing conflict is going to be much more difficult than restoring them temporarily. Iran has demonstrated that it can threaten commercial shipping without completely shutting down Hormuz, and neither tanker escorts nor limited military operations offer an obvious permanent solution to that problem.

That's ultimately why I remain skeptical that another short bombing campaign would fundamentally change the situation. Washington either has to negotiate a settlement that likely involves substantial concessions to Iran, pursue a much larger and riskier military confrontation, or tolerate a prolonged stalemate in which shipping remains expensive and vulnerable. I don't see an especially easy way for the administration to present any of those outcomes as a decisive victory.

Meanwhile, prices just keep moving higher. WTI has now finished above $103, Brent is approaching $117, and crude backwardation continues to strengthen. There's certainly a geopolitical risk premium in these prices, but I'm still not convinced the possibility of another major round of fighting is fully reflected in the market. My outlook remains for crude to stay elevated unless there's a genuine de-escalation, with substantial upside risk if the conflict expands again.

text:
It occurred to me today that your children, no matter what you teach them, the schools you send them do, the experiences you offer them, the example you give them -- no matter how curated and perfect it may be -- nothing can prevent them from assuming the 'character' of the culture of the geography they grow up in. 

It's like the stone you're seeking to sculpt. 

You can carve, even your children -- once full grown adults -- can carve it, but you can never change the stone. 

As an adult, you can never fully change this character. 

Me, being from a hill-billy Wisconsin family, no matter how hard I would try -- I could put my whole being into the endeavor -- will I ever be able to fully become like someone raised in Dallas, or Nashville, or New Orleans, or NYC.

It is simply not possible. 

Where you're born and raised IS part of you and it cannot be changed. 

This realization has made me realize the importance of place and location more than anything else. 

Even if you have a strong community in a bad place, that character imprints on your children. 

If your location is made of atomized people, yet you spend time with families from your church, on Sundays, and maybe even once or twice during the week, you're kids are still going to inherit that atomized character in some way. 

This is why it matters so much to pour effort into your place. If you're set on staying, you must build. You must do what you can to shape your place, so that future generations will have a better place. 

What's mind blowing is, that no matter how much you as an individual do to change that place, it won't change unless the vast majority of the people (i'm talking 80-90%) also change. 

To me, this is a hint at why it matters so much to care for your neighbor.

text:
SHE BECAME A HERO OF THE SOVIET UNION IN 22, AND HITLER CALLED HER HIS PERSONAL ENEMY
We are talking about the legendary Soviet intelligence officer Nadezhda Troyan.
Nadezhda Viktorovna Troyan was born on October 24, 1921 in the Belarusian town of Drissa, Vitebsk region, which later became Verkhnedvinsky.
Father - Victor Troyan - fought in World War I, was a cavalier of the George Cross, and then received the profession of an accountant and worked on various manufactures.
Mother Evdokiya Grigorievna led the farming. Interestingly, Troyan translated from Belarusian is a fork with three teeth. According to the memories of the son of the scout, she was very proud of her Belarusian origin.
But Trojan didn't live long in Belarus as a child. Her parents went looking for money with children - Nadia had another younger brother Zhenya - across the country. The family lived in Irkutsk and Kansk, Voronezh and Grozny. The girl constantly changed schools. And then the family settled for a while in Krasnoyarsk, where Nadia enrolled in the school named after the 20th anniversary of Komsomol.
She studied great, was an activist, loved hiking, was always surrounded by fans. Interestingly, Boria Galushkin studied with her in a parallel class - the same Boris Galushkin, whom she will meet later, in the war.
The girl showed non-dozen language abilities and learned German as a native one. She'll need this later.
Nadezhda graduated with a red certificate and could choose any university. She joined the sanitary faculty of the 1th Moscow Medical Institute - students of this faculty, unlike ′′ therapeutic workers ", were provided with a dormitory. But then she transferred to study in Minsk, where her father was offered a job at the chocolate factory ′′ Bolshevichka ".
That's where the war began, Minsk was occupied. Nazis organized a concentration camp at the place where they used to spend time with their classmates.
Nadia came there with her girlfriends and threw pieces of bread through the barbed wire, or rags so that prisoners quench their thirst.
The girls even, oddly enough, managed to organize several camp escapes.
Nadezhda later began to write and distribute leaflets. And at 1942 a family, to avoid theft to Germany, moved to Smolevichy town 40 kilometers from Minsk, where Trojan was issued an invoice for the office of Peat Factory.
She dreamed of connecting with partisans and suggested that her friend, nurse Nyura Kosarevskaya, was involved in this movement. But Nyura didn't ′′ split ".
Once Trojan accidentally heard a conversation in German, which should have stated that the next day a punitive operation was scheduled to destroy the squad. She urgently warned Nyura, and the squad managed to escape. A week later, a friend told Troyan that partisans wanted to meet her.
The girl had to come to the forest glade, stand up near the oak and whistle three times. But she didn't know how to whistle, and took the police whistle with her. No one showed up for a long time: the guerrillas first decided that the police whistle it. After all, one of the fighters of the partisan squad ′′ Storm ", which is part of the intelligence and sabotage ′′ Uncle Koli's Brigade ′′ and headed by the senior state security major Petr Grigorievich Shopatin.
As a result, the whole Troyan family moved into the intelligence and sabotage ′′ Uncle Kolya's Brigade. Nadina was preparing for the fighters, her father was ′′ on the farm ". Hope, who got into the storm squad, had to shoot the machine gun, and participate in rail operations (for 2,5 military years, Uncle Koli's Brigade let in Belarus under the derailment of 328 enemy echelons, but mines had to be installed under the very nose of fascists), perform intelligence tasks and provide medical assistance to the wounded.
In 1943, her meeting happened with the same Boris Galushkin. Troyan crossed the river on logs and suddenly saw that some young man was rocking them. She got angry, but suddenly found out Boris, who was a paratrooped in the OMSBON squad in the same unit where Hope was. Galushkin will die in a year...
In February 1943, Stalin ordered the destruction of Hitler's substitutes in Ukraine and in Belarus - respectively Erich Koch and Wilhelm von Cuba. The latter was known for his atrocities - in a couple of years of his reign in Belarus, 400 thousand people were destroyed.
206,5 thousand died in Trostenets concentration camp alone, not to mention the victims of Khatyn. Cuba was exactly saying: ′′ We need only mentioning one of my names to trembling Russian and Belarusian so that their brains will be frozen when they hear ′′ Wilhelm Cube ". I ask you, faithful subjects of the great Führer, to help me with this ".
The hunt for the criminal was conducted by more than ten different units - both from the NKVD special units, from the Red Army intelligence and partisan squads. Many attempts have been made - undermines, poisoning, but in vain...
In the ′′ Uncle Koly ′′ team, the state security major Ivan Zolotar was instructed to lead the operation. It was decided to look for approaches to the mansion where Cuba lived. The situation in Minsk was difficult at the time, the streets were moving only on special passes, thorough inspections were conducted. The Cuba mansion was also carefully guarded.
Then Troyan, who kept in touch with Minsk underground members, was given a very dangerous order - to infiltrate the house at all costs. However, the girl was often given the most difficult errands - she had a special talent of entering into trust in people and the ability to place them in her own way. Plus the mentioned brilliant knowledge of German and amazing, celebrated by all the coolness.
The intelligence officer moved to Minsk and established relations with Tatiana Kalita, a maid in a cherished mansion.
She pointed to Elena Mazannik, also a maid in the house, - she was beautiful (and Cuba was weak for the female sex). Mazannik had long treated Trojan with distrust and feared the consequences.
But then she compiled a scheme of the location of the rooms in the mansion at the request of Trojan and provided her with other necessary information that was transferred to the military intelligence unit ′′ Uncle Dima's Squad ".
In September 1943, his participant Maria Osipova handed over an English magnetic mine with an hour mechanism attached to the springs of Cuba's bed. There was an explosion at night.
And at this time Troyan made her way to the closed city already with the second mines I hid in the cake. She was satisfied with checks and searches, and found nothing. Upon arrival, the reconnaissance saw that the wanted person who had carried out an attempt.
Troyan understood that the mine needed to be rid of - the risk was too high, but such English miniature mines were very short of guerrillas, and she did not. She was lucky to have Slovaks at the exit of the city, not Germans. They will join the squad later.
It was after the murder of Cuba, in honor of which mourning was declared in Germany, Hitler declared all the participants of the operation - Trojan, Mazannik and Osipov - as his personal enemies.
The girls were first sent to a distant farm on the way back, and then to the capital.
All Troyan's close ones remained in the forest, her mom - Evdokiya Grigorievna was even awarded a medal ′′ Partisan of the Great Patriotic War ".
And on October 29, 1943, Nadezhda Troyan, Elena Mazanik and Maria Osipova were awarded the title of Heroes of the Soviet Union. During the war, only 87 women were given this title. Nadezhda Trojan was later awarded with the orders of the Red Banner, Patriotic War, Red Star, Friendship of Nations and medals.
After the Victory, she came to study again at the Sechenov Institute, in 1947 she received a diploma, married a military correspondent Vasily Koroteev, who worked on the frontline with Konstantin Simonov, gave birth to two sons, the youngest of whom Alexei later became a famous cardiac surgeon.
Later she became the vice-rector of her own institute, Associate Professor of the Department of Hospital Surgery. In 1961, she defended her thesis on ′′ Restoration operations on non-baked galls ", and in 1967 headed the Central Election Commission of Sanitary Education. At the same time, she was involved in both clinical and experimental surgery. Troyan has had many animal surgeries, working out the device for sewing and plastic gall flow.
However, even such an intense work was not enough for her - Troyan actively engaged in public activities, worked in war veterans and the protection of peace, from whom she spoke abroad with reports.
She was also chairman of the Executive Committee of the Union of Red Cross and Red Crescent of the USSR, a member of the Council of the International Federation of Resistance Fighters, co-chairman of the International Organization of sanitary education. And at least once a year she tried to be in her native Belarus.
Nadezhda Troyan died on September 7, 2011, at the age of 89 They buried her at the Troyekurovsky cemetery.
The heroine's name was awarded to the capital school No. 1288, where her son studied, and last year at the building of the First Moscow Medical University named after him. Sechenov opened a memorial board.

text:
WEIRD ANIMAL FACTS
The Bizarre Tale of the Beer Drinking, Nazi Fighting Bear of World War II

During World War II, Poland was at the mercy of the relentless drive against them orchestrated by both Germany and the Soviet Union, who killed, looted, stole land, oppressed, and imprisoned the Polish indiscriminately. The normally up to that point peaceful Poles had no choice but to be dragged into ferocious battle, where they faced execution and a life of hard labor in Soviet gulags if captured. When Germany eventually turned on the Red Army, Stalin made the decision to release thousands of Polish POWs in the hopes that they would go out to do battle with the Germans, but the Polish sided with the British instead.

In 1942, a military unit from Polish Armed Forces in the East, also called the Anders Army, set out from the Soviet Union towards Iran, along with thousands of these disgruntled refugees who had been put to grueling hard labor at the Soviet gulags. This ragtag group made their way to Iran, where they would form the 22nd Artillery Supply Company of the Polish Second Army Corps. Their ultimate mission was to continue on to Palestine, where they hoped to join forces with the British 8th Army and assist in the Allied invasion of Italy. On their way to Tehran, a group of Polish soldiers came across a young Iranian boy in the Hamadan Province, who had curiously found an orphaned Syrian brown bear cub whose mother had been killed by hunters and which he carried about in a simple sack. The soldiers became enamored with the bear, and offered to buy it for a mere couple of tins of corned beef.

The bear became adopted by the men of the Polish Second Army Corps, who named it Wojtek, which roughly translates to 'he who enjoys war,’ ‘happy warrior,’ ‘joyful warrior,’ or 'smiling warrior'. At first the bear was malnourished and in poor health, and had to be nursed back to health with condensed milk from a cleaned out old vodka bottle, which graduated to treats of marmalade and honey. When Wojtek had regained his health and vigor, he quickly enamored himself to the soldiers and became a sort of unofficial mascot of the company. The huge bear was uncommonly tame and friendly, known to sit around the campfire with the men, sleep in their tents, eat with them, and engage in playful wrestling matches with them, all the while remaining a gentle companion even as his size skyrocketed to around 1,000 pounds and a height of over 6 feet. All in all, the hulking bear was treated just like anyone else in the unit, and most forgot the fact that he was a massive, potentially dangerous animal. To them he was one of their own.

One of Wojtek’s most unusual attributes was his penchant for drinking beer, which was doled out as a reward, as well as his habit of chain smoking the cigarettes which the entertained men steadily provided him. He also was quite fond of taking hot baths and showers, and even learned how to operate the water taps. The unusual bear was also known to march alongside the soldiers on two feet, ride around in jeeps with his massive head hanging out of the passenger window, and stand up to salute passing soldiers when greeted. All of this further endeared him to the Polish soldiers, and offered a much needed boost of morale for the men, who had been toiling about in the harsh desert conditions. One of the men would later say of this:

“What the bear offered all of these men was comfort. At a time when they were far from home, had nothing, and often no-one, Wojtek stood in for the wives, children, pets, family they’d left behind. He was someone to love and someone who loved them back.”

Wojtek would become quite the attraction among the soldiers, civilians, and locals alike, and seemed to make friends wherever he went on the unit’s trek to Iraq, Syria, Palestine and Egypt. He even started to prove his usefulness, when he allegedly cornered an Arab spy in a bathhouse, which led to his capture and the subsequent extraction of key information, which catapulted Wojtek from a pet to a hero. In Egypt on April 14, 1944, as they prepared to head out to Naples to join the British forces in their assault on Italian and German forces, the Polish unit faced a conundrum. The rules at the time forbade the presence of any animals or pets, only soldiers, so it at first seemed as though the men would be forced to say goodbye to their beloved companion. However, to get around this rule, it was decided to officially actually enlist Wojtek into the military as a private, and soon after a corporal, making him a fully legal member of the Polish military. The quick-thinking, improvised plan worked, authorization was granted, and Private Wojtek joined the rest of his unit on their dangerous journey ahead as an equal.

Upon arrival in Naples, the British official for the British Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery, an Archibald Brown, was in for quite a surprise as he processed the incoming Polish unit. After talking to the rest of the disembarking men, he noticed that there was still one soldier who had not made his acquaintance, a Corporal Wojtek. The mysterious colonel had a service serial number and pay book, but seemed to have simply vanished. When numerous efforts to call out to the missing soldier produced no response, an exasperated Archibald is said to have asked the Polish where the man had gone, to which another Polish colonel is said to have responded "Well, he only understands Polish and Persian,” before leading the puzzled British official to the cage containing the bear. Interestingly, the British just sort of shrugged their shoulders and went along with it.

From here, Wojtek would prove his worth as he carried heavy supplies and artillery shells about for the Polish during the fierce battle for Monte Cassino, which had proved to be one of the bloodiest and horrific battles of the Western Front. Wojtek bravely and dutifully used his vast strength to lug extremely heavy packs and munitions from the supply trucks to the men on the front lines, completely unfazed by the loud cacophony of war blasting about all around him, and he became lauded as a loyal hero. So respected was this courageous bear that the official insignia of the 22nd Artillery was made into the image of a bear carrying a large Howitzer shell in order to honor him. It is unclear just what the befuddled German and Italian forces must have thought of the intimidating sight of a massive brown bear tirelessly carrying about supplies for the enemy, but it was probably fairly demoralizing. Wojtek’s reputation subsequently became almost legendary.

The Polish and their allies would eventually break through to capture Monte Cassino, and continue their fight up and down the Italian peninsula. When the war came to a close in 1945, the 22nd Company was brought to Berwickshire, Scotland, to be stationed at Winfield Airfield, along with their beloved brown bear Wojtek, who had survived the ordeal and was seemingly none the worse for wear. The curious sight made Wojtek a sensation among locals and the media, and he was even made an honorary member of the Polish-Scottish Association. When the unit was inevitably demobilized, Wojtek faced an uncertain future, as no one was quite sure what to do with a large brown bear. It was decided that he would be donated to the Edinburgh Zoo, where he would spend the remainder of his days.

During his time at the zoo, Wojtek became a huge attraction, drawing crowds of people, and he remained in the spotlight, being frequently visited by news crews and TV shows, as well as becoming a sort of symbol of the solidarity between Scotland and Poland. He was also sometimes visited by his old comrades in arms, to whom the bear would respond to by waving and pricking his ears up when he heard Polish. One former soldier who had served with the bear described one visit thus:

“As soon as I mentioned his name, he would sit on his backside and shake his head wanting a cigarette.”

Some of the men who had served with Wojtek secretly threw the cigarettes to their old companion, who would sadly just gulp them down in the absence of anyone to light them for him. A few of these old comrades were said to have even gone into the enclosure, where the bear would welcome them and wrestle with them just like old times. In December of 1963, Wojtek would finally pass way at the age of 21. After Wojtek’s death, several monuments were erected in his honor, including plaques in the Imperial War Museum in London and at the Canadian War Museum in Ottawa. In November of 2011, veterans and bagpipe players converged upon Edinburgh for a commemorative celebration which included a eulogy in Polish for the war hero bear. On the 70th anniversary of the Battle of Monte Cassino, on 7 November, 2015, a large, £300,000 bronze statue of Wojtek designed by sculptor Alan Beattie Herriot was erected in the center of Edinburgh in the city's Princes Street Gardens, which depicts the bear and soldier Peter Prendys, who was often seen as his closest companion. Additionally, Wojteks’s unique history has been reproduced in numerous books and films, including the 2011 BBC documentary, Wojtek – The Bear That Went to War.

It is easy when looking back through the horrors of World War II to focus on all of the death and violence. The scale of the whole thing invites it, pulling us in with its myriad tales of death, desolation, and abject evil. Yet scattered through this domain of vicious fighting and mass destruction there are those that serve to touch us with their warmth and surprise us with their bizarreness. The tale of Wojtek the bear truly counts as one of the odder stories to pass through the history of World War II, almost surreal in its ability to meld the fighting with warmth, humor, and companionship. Wojtek the bear was a rarity in this world, a symbol of solidarity, morale, and hope, that came shining through the fog of war to guide those who would fight. It gives us hope that in our darkest hour, when we seem most alone, there can be a beacon that keeps us together and guides us, no matter what form that may take. In the annals of truly unique war stories, that of Wojtek the bear truly stands out as one of the stranger and more touching.

text:
In 1941, a Spaniard walked into the British embassy in Madrid and offered to spy on the Nazis.

The British turned him down.

So he went to the Germans instead, pretended to be a loyal fascist, and got hired as a German spy. His plan was to lie to them for the rest of the war.

It worked better than anyone could have imagined.

His name was Juan Pujol García. Before the war he had tried his hand at running a chicken farm and a movie theater. He had no spy training. What he had was a deep hatred of both fascism and communism after the Spanish Civil War, and an incredible imagination.

The Germans gave him a codename, invisible ink, money, and orders to go to Britain and recruit spies.

He didn't go to Britain.

He went to Lisbon, Portugal, and made everything up.

Using a tourist guidebook, maps, magazines, newsreels, and a British railway timetable from the library, he wrote long, detailed reports about life in England. Military movements. Morale. Ports.

He'd never been there. He made mistakes. He didn't understand British money. He once reported that dockworkers in Glasgow would do anything for a liter of wine.

The Germans loved him anyway.

Then British codebreakers reading German messages noticed something strange. The Germans were hunting for a convoy that didn't exist, based on a report from some agent in Britain they'd never heard of.

The British went looking for this mystery spy. They found Pujol. In 1942 they finally took him on and brought him to London.

Now he had real help. MI5 gave him the codename Garbo, after the actress, because they thought he was the greatest actor in the world.

Together with his British handler, Pujol built a fake spy network for the Germans. It eventually had 27 imaginary agents. Each had a name, a personality, a job, and a backstory. A Welsh nationalist. A Venezuelan student. A Greek sailor. Some of them recruited their own imaginary sub-agents.

When they needed to explain why one agent had gone quiet, they killed him off. They even put a fake obituary in a Liverpool newspaper. The Germans reportedly paid a pension to his widow.

Who also didn't exist.

Then came D-Day.

Hours before the landings, the British let Pujol send a message warning the Germans that the invasion was coming in Normandy. It was timed so it would arrive too late to matter, but it made him look brilliant.

Three days later he sent the most important message of his career. Normandy was a trick, he said. The real invasion was still coming, at Calais, led by a huge army under General Patton.

That army was fake too. But the Germans believed him.

German forces that could have been rushed to Normandy were held back near Calais for weeks, waiting for an attack that never came.

The Germans were so grateful they awarded him the Iron Cross.

A few months later, King George VI made him a Member of the Order of the British Empire.

He's one of the only people known to have been decorated by both sides of the war.

After the war, afraid of revenge from surviving Nazis, he faked his own death from malaria in Africa and disappeared to Venezuela, where he lived quietly running a shop.

For decades the world thought he was dead.

In 1984, a British writer tracked him down. Pujol came back to Normandy for the 40th anniversary of D-Day and met veterans who had landed on the beaches.

Some of them thanked him.

text:
Orcus has a long history of turning somebody else's desperation into something he can use. That runs through his earlier rule in Myst and his work for the Dark Horde. He can lead an army, but he's just as willing to make an offer that puts frightened people in a terrible position.

His older connection to Shang begins with the story of a farmer and his daughters. Orcus and his queen rule Myst, and the farmer is desperate for a successful harvest. The bargain offered to him sounds simple: a flower each year for seven years. The meaning turns out to be his daughters, whose lives are taken to increase Orcus's power.

Shang becomes involved when the last daughter is threatened. The souls of the daughters have been connected to seven ravens, and they help him confront the rulers. The daughters are restored, and the youngest, Allexa, becomes Shang's wife. Orcus is therefore tied to a part of Shang's life that reaches much further back than the current war around Sela.

Later, Orcus is one of the Dark One's important generals. He has his own interest in regaining control of Myst, and that makes his work for the Horde more than taking orders from somebody else's throne. He knows the place they're fighting over, and he has reasons of his own to want power there again.

The attack on Tallus is one of the clearest examples of his methods. He offers to spare the city's children if the people hand over Sela, Blake, and Bolder. It forces the people inside to think about surrendering their possible defenders to protect their families. He's trying to make fear do part of the work before the army attacks.

He also has Gruel serving him. Giving Gruel the Shadow Dragon Claw puts a much bigger threat into that battle, allowing him to transform into a shadow dragon. Orcus is using a follower's abilities and giving him a weapon that makes him more dangerous. It takes the efforts of Sela and her allies to bring that creature down.

Even the aftermath has another act of cruelty waiting in it. Orcus takes one of Blake's arrows and uses its magic against King William. A weapon that belonged to one of the defenders becomes the means of killing someone on their side. Winning the immediate confrontation doesn't stop him from looking for another opening.

His role in Belinda's past is just as important. He's the one who took her baby on the Dark One's orders. That action helps shape years of harm for somebody who doesn't know the truth of what happened. Orcus can damage a person's life in a way that keeps working long after he's left the scene.

Then there's his mission to help restore the Dark Queen. While Blake and Bolder are trying to rebuild the council, Orcus is pursuing something that could make the opposition even stronger. His part in the story keeps crossing from old personal history into the larger conflict. Shang and Belinda have reasons to hate him that have nothing to do with merely standing on the other side of a battlefield.

🇭🇹🇸🇻 À ceux qui pensent que Nayib Bukele peut intervenir militairement en Haïti à la suite de la «disparition » des quatre militaires salvadoriens, je tiens à rappeler ceci :

La volonté légitime du président salvadorien de sauver ses quatre militaires ne saurait justifier une intervention militaire unilatérale en Haïti, en violation de sa souveraineté nationale.

La lutte contre les gangs ne saurait devenir un prétexte pour contourner le droit international. Toute opération militaire doit s’inscrire dans un cadre juridique clairement établi, conformément au mandat de la Force de répression des gangs (FRG) et aux dispositions de la Charte des Nations unies.

La gravité de la situation sécuritaire en Haïti ne suspend ni le droit international ni la souveraineté du pays.

NEW DELHI, INDIA - Mozambique's reference to its ports may prove more consequential than the discussion about rice imports. Rice already flows from India to Mozambique; the bigger shift would be turning Mozambique from a destination market into a distribution platform. That changes the commercial logic for Indian exporters, processors and logistics firms, giving them a potential base for serving multiple Southern African countries instead of negotiating each market separately.

For Mozambique, agro-processing offers a way to capture more value from imports and agricultural production rather than remaining a transit point. If investment follows, competition among regional transport corridors could intensify, because cargo tends to concentrate around the ports and routes that offer the lowest total cost. The proposal creates a new expectation that trade infrastructure, not just commodity supply, must now carry a larger share of the India-Mozambique relationship.

text:
Bukidnon’s vast pineapple plantations began in 1926, when an American company turned to Mindanao to establish what would become one of the world’s largest pineapple operations

The seemingly endless rows of pineapple plants covering Bukidnon’s rolling highlands have become one of the province’s most recognizable landscapes. But few realize that this agricultural empire traces its origins to a crisis thousands of kilometers away, in Hawaii.

During the 1920s, Hawaii dominated the global pineapple industry. However, rising land costs, agricultural diseases, and competition with sugar plantations prompted American companies to seek alternative growing locations.

Among them was the California Packing Corporation, popularly known as Calpak, which marketed products under the Del Monte brand.

WHY BUKIDNON?

The Philippines was then an American colony, making it an attractive destination for US agricultural investments.

Company researchers discovered that Bukidnon’s elevated terrain, fertile soil, favorable rainfall, and relatively low exposure to destructive typhoons offered excellent conditions for pineapple cultivation.

In 1926, the Philippine Packing Corporation began planting pineapples in Bukidnon, reportedly using pineapple crowns imported from Hawaii.

What began as an experimental venture eventually expanded into thousands of hectares of plantations.

By the 1930s, tractors and mechanized farming equipment were transforming the highlands into vast agricultural fields. Camp Phillips in Manolo Fortich became a major plantation center, while Bugo in Cagayan de Oro developed into a processing hub.

THE DARKER SIDE OF EXPANSION

The industry’s growth also came with controversy.

American colonial laws restricted corporate access to public agricultural lands, but government-backed leasing arrangements helped large plantation enterprises expand.

The conversion of land into plantations, alongside government-sponsored migration, also placed pressure on Indigenous communities whose ancestral territories had existed long before the arrival of American corporations.

A GLOBAL PINEAPPLE POWERHOUSE

Despite destruction during World War II, the industry recovered and expanded as pineapple production in Hawaii became increasingly expensive.

Today, Del Monte’s operations across Bukidnon and neighboring Misamis Oriental cover approximately 30,000 hectares, forming one of the world’s major integrated pineapple production complexes.

Nearly a century after its beginnings, Bukidnon remains widely celebrated as the “Pineapple Capital of Asia,” a legacy shaped by fertile land, colonial history, corporate ambition, and generations of Filipino agricultural workers.

(✍️: Top Dagohoy)

HOUSTON WE HAVE A FCKNG PROBLEM ?

THE GREAT AMERICAN MAGIC TRICK: NOW YOU’RE RICH!

A fictional financial fairy tale.

ACT I: THE INVISIBLE PIGGY BANK

Folks, gather around! In tonight's spectacular, the government has discovered enough money to make everyone rich.

Where was it? Behind the Pentagon's couch?

Apparently, they confiscated the bad guys' fortunes. Drug money! Fraud money! Yacht money from people who thought “offshore” meant taxes couldn't swim!

Then came the oil, the gold, the minerals—everything underground except my missing retirement prospects.

“It belongs to the nation!”

Wonderful. I belong to the nation. Can I have twenty bucks?

“Don't get political.”

ACT II: THE DEBT DISAPPEARS

Now the salesman leans forward:

"Remember those terrifying trillions in debt? A sizable chunk was imaginary!"

Imaginary? My bank charged me thirty-five actual dollars for being six imaginary dollars short!

I once disputed a restaurant charge. They wanted receipts, dates, identification, and apparently a surviving witness. These guys erase trillions with a microphone and dramatic background music.

According to the pitch, they'll use real confiscated assets to settle supposedly fake obligations.

That's some trick: the rabbit disappears, the hat gets audited, and the magician retreats to an island.

ACT III: YOU’RE RICH! ACCESS SOLD SEPARATELY

Here comes your reward: shares in a magnificent sovereign wealth fund!

In this miraculous offer, you can't sell them.
You can't redeem them.
You can't spend them.

But they're YOURS!

So is the moon in my vacation photographs. Neither one pays the electric bill.

I tried explaining my theoretical fortune to the landlord.

“Congratulations,” he said. “Your theoretical apartment is available immediately. Vacate the physical one by Friday.”

They're handing a hungry man a photograph of a sandwich.

"Look at that cheese! You're practically full!"

ACT IV: THE WEALTH EXPERIENCE

You'll still drive the same coughing car, dodge the same potholes, and spend forty minutes telling a medical billing robot you're a human being.

But somewhere, on a dashboard nobody can explain, you'll be a millionaire.

Your assets will be soaring.
Your checking account will be wheezing.
Your dentist will still want cash.

And when do you die?

The richest corpse in the cemetery!

Cardboard coffin. Premium portfolio.

Your headstone:

HERE LIES A SHAREHOLDER.
NET WORTH: ASTRONOMICAL.
AVAILABLE BALANCE: ASK AGAIN LATER.

FINALE: SANITIZED FOR YOUR PROTECTION

Relax. The pitch has been washed, polished, pasteurized, and stripped of dangerous contaminants—like evidence, questions, and a withdrawal button.

Just smile. Accept your invisible fortune.

And remember: if you're still broke, that's your fault.

You keep insisting on spending the money.

NOTHING CAN STOP WHAT IS COMING.

HOUSTON, THE PROBLEM IS THAT IT DOESN'T HAVE A DATE ON THE CALENDARS.  

W.T.F.

FOURTEEN EMAILS IN 4 MONTHS: RECORDS SHOW MASTERSON'S WORK AT ALLEGED 'NO-SHOW JOB'
ONE-SENTENCE SUMMARY Newly released Wichita State University records show that Kansas Senate President and gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson sent just 14 university emails over four months while holding a highly compensated director position, raising questions about his responsibilities, compensation, and potential political conflicts of interest.
KEY TAKEAWAYS
•Limited email activity: Masterson sent 14 university emails over four months, compared with 532 sent by his assistant director.
•Extensive redactions: More than 17 of the 26 pages released were blank or entirely redacted, limiting public scrutiny.
•Substantial compensation: Masterson received $163,000 in 2025 and more than $1.1 million over the past decade. The position's planned 2027 salary is $241,781.
•Limited documented activities: Readable messages concerned a trailer, an audit information request, calendar records, and a biographical correction.
•Private calendar: Masterson acknowledged keeping most work and personal appointments on a private calendar.
•Disputed work expectations: Masterson describes a flexible schedule. A GoCreate mentor confirms seeing him occasionally at the facility.
•Financial transparency: WSU declined to provide a detailed funding breakdown, although Masterson maintains that state tax dollars do not support his compensation.
•Political implications: Holscher alleges improper political influence. Masterson's campaign rejects that characterization.
•Unresolved question: The available emails do not establish how many hours Masterson worked or whether his compensation was justified by his responsibilities and results.
ARTICLE SUMMARY Matthew Kelly reports that newly released Wichita State University records provide a limited picture of Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson's work as director of GoCreate, a makerspace supported partly by the Koch Family Foundation. The records have become an issue in Masterson's campaign for governor amid allegations that he holds a highly paid "no-show job," which he denies.
Between April 11 and August 10, 2026, Masterson sent 14 emails from his university account, according to WSU's general counsel. Assistant Director Kimberly McCollum sent 532 during the same period. The university provided 26 pages of responsive records, but more than 17 were blank or entirely redacted. Only four of Masterson's messages were readable, limiting what the disclosure can establish about his broader activities.
The visible messages offered modest examples of work. Masterson forwarded a request for information about software costs for an audit, sent McCollum a link to a trailer for sale, and corrected a university biography that incorrectly claimed he graduated from Kansas State University. In a separate exchange, he asked WSU to delay releasing his calendars until he could review personal entries with an attorney. He said he maintained most work and personal appointments on a private calendar.
GoCreate, located at WSU's John Bardo Center, offers access to equipment and studios for design, fabrication and entrepreneurship. Masterson's campaign says more than 2,000 people have held memberships since 2017. Part-time mentor Bill Carey said he occasionally sees Masterson on site and considers the "no-show" accusation unfair. Masterson has described a flexible schedule, sometimes working in person two or three days a week and sometimes not at all.
State records show Masterson received $163,000 from WSU in 2025 and more than $1.1 million over the past decade. The director position's budgeted base salary would rise by more than $24,000 to $241,781 in 2027, although his campaign says he would leave the job if elected governor. He takes unpaid leave during legislative sessions and announced leave for the remainder of his campaign.

text:
Nina Simone's high school kept no record that she ever went there. Allen in Asheville took Black girls out of mountain counties that had not built them one, and it took her in from Tryon. When the place shut, no records of the school were maintained. Not hers, not anybody's.

What the building did turn out, every spring for its first four decades, was a line of girls in dresses they had made themselves. It was a requirement and it held from the earliest classes until sometime in the nineteen thirties. The principal who wrote it down, Julia Titus, listed it between the spring singing festival and the running total of graduates.

The school that produced Nina Simone was built to teach Black girls housekeeping.

The women who ran Allen in Asheville wanted a home where girls would learn to keep house and improve conditions in their own. Eunice Waymon boarded there and walked out of it as valedictorian in 1950. She was not the strangest thing that came out of that building.

What came out of it, every spring for the school's first four decades, was a line of girls in dresses they had made themselves.

It was a requirement and it held from the earliest classes until sometime in the nineteen thirties. The principal who wrote it down, Julia Titus, listed it between the spring singing festival and the running total of graduates.

The Asheville Citizen-Times printed the arithmetic in January 1942. Of the twenty-seven counties in western North Carolina, seven had accredited high schools for Black students, seven had schools the state would not stand behind, and the rest had nothing at all.

Fifty-three girls were boarding at Allen that same month. Twenty-eight of them had come out of nine of the state's western counties, nineteen more from other North Carolina counties or from states next door, and the rest from further off than that.

That same newspaper counted Allen as one of only three private accredited secondary schools for African Americans anywhere in North Carolina.

Allen's girls came from counties the oral histories name. Cherokee, Clay, Swain, Yancey and Polk, where high school facilities for Black youth were inadequate or did not exist at all.

A girl from any of them who wanted to finish school was looking at a dormitory in Asheville, fifty or a hundred miles down the mountain from her mother's kitchen.

The building at the other end of that trip had started life as a livery stable.

L. M. Pease and his wife Ann Pinney Pease spent years doing Methodist mission work among the poor in New York City before they retired to the North Carolina mountains around 1875. They bought property near Beaucatcher Mountain and converted the stable into a school. Three Black teachers lived in a small cottage on the same lot, and children came during the day while adults came at night.

Their health failed quickly. In July 1887 the Peases handed the whole property to the Woman's Home Missionary Society of the Methodist Episcopal Church.

The school opened on October 31, 1887, with two teachers, the Reverend N. S. Albright and Alsie B. Dole. Dole stayed thirty-three years, teacher and then superintendent until 1920.

Three students came the first morning.

By the end of that month a hundred and three were enrolled. By the close of the first year the number had passed two hundred, and the first grade held three generations of one family, two preachers, and more than twenty married men and women. They brought their own books from home, mostly Bibles and blue-back spellers, and the principal's history records that they were anxious to read, and especially to read their Bibles.

What the Society built to answer that demand was narrower than what had come through the door.

In 1896 the school stopped taking all comers and became a residential preparatory school for Black women.

The historian Jamie Butcher argues that the narrowing tracked two things at once, a Black public school opening in Asheville and a turn toward single-sex education inside the Methodist Episcopal Church. Allen dropped its early grades as public schools took them over, and kept the girls.

Keeping them meant housing them. An Englishwoman touring the South visited the school and offered a thousand dollars if the Society would build that home at once. It was done, and the home was dedicated on February 9, 1897, carrying her family name.

In 1905 another visitor gave two thousand dollars for a building to replace the stable, and it included a chapel that served as this neighborhood's Methodist church for eighteen years and stands today as Berry Temple.

Boys kept coming until 1941. The girls boarded.

Board, room and tuition ran thirteen dollars and fifty cents a month through the depression.

More than half the dormitory girls stayed on campus through Christmas because nobody at home could cover the trip, and the teachers were asked to stay with them and could not afford to travel either, on a cash salary of thirty dollars a month.

So the girls spent December in Asheville in a dark blue jumper, a pongee blouse and a plain black coat, in hats bought from the school. Each year they wrote essays on prohibition for the Methodist temperance board, and the local temperance union handed out a five dollar prize.

Then in the spring, the ones who were graduating sewed.

The needlework had gone into the curriculum to make them useful in other people's houses and competent in their own. Allen ran a Beauty Culture course for one stretch of years and a Teacher Training Course for another, an extra year of work that qualified a graduate to teach.

What the sewing produced was a garment marking the end of something the state had refused to provide. At commencement the entire student body recited a passage of scripture in unison, and then the graduates walked in clothes they had cut and stitched themselves.

The diploma those dresses were worn for kept getting heavier. Allen became a four-year high school with state accreditation in 1924, the year Mr. and Mrs. F. A. Arter of Cleveland paid for another wing. The Southern Association accredited it in 1940, and in June 1945 the name officially became Allen High School.

The first class had graduated in 1899. There were four girls in it, and one of the four, Isabelle Jones, came back and taught at Allen for forty-three years.

For much of that time Jones ran a spiritual festival every April at Hopkins Chapel A.M.E. Zion Church, with buses bringing children in from miles around Asheville to sing on a Sunday afternoon. Titus wrote that the singing was for the joy of it and not in competition. That sentence is close to everything the record kept about Isabelle Jones.

By the nineteen fifties the school was sending half of every graduating class to college.

Christine Mann Darden came to Allen from Monroe, on the far side of the state, and finished top of her class in 1958. She has said since that her interest in mathematics began there, with an Allen teacher named Ruth Walther.

Darden went on to Hampton, then to NASA, then to a doctorate in mechanical engineering. She became the first Black woman promoted into the Senior Executive Service at NASA Langley, and Margot Lee Shetterly put her in Hidden Figures.

Andrea Lawrence of the class of 1964 became a computer scientist. When the alumnae gathered years later, the newspaper listing Allen's graduates named an ophthalmologist, a professor at A and T who wrote books, and a woman working as administrative assistant to the White House press secretary.

An aerodynamicist, a composer and a computer scientist came out of that dormitory, and it ran on thirteen dollars and fifty cents a month.

In the spring of 1957 a ninth grader at Allen named Judy Genier received a letter of commendation from Mamie Eisenhower. The First Lady of the United States was congratulating her for being the first white student ever enrolled at the school.

Judy Genier's home was in New York State, and she spent the eighth, ninth and tenth grades at Allen.

Five months after that letter, in September 1957, a fifteen-year-old named Dorothy Counts walked into Harry Harding High School in Charlotte through a crowd that spat on her and threw things. She lasted four days. Nobody in Washington wrote to her, and her father took her out.

Several accounts of her life have her finishing her schooling at Allen, though the Charlotte reporting from the time follows her only as far as Pennsylvania.

Two children crossed in opposite directions in the same state in the same year. A white child moving into a Black school was a national courtesy. A Black child moving the other way was a riot.

The counties did eventually build what they had refused to build.

Public high schools opened to Black students across western North Carolina through the sixties, and the families who had been sending thirteen-year-olds down the mountain stopped sending them. Enrollment fell.

Ruth Walther, the mathematics teacher who had set Christine Darden going, was the principal by then. She gave the reason in one sentence.

They could not charge the tuition they needed to keep the school running.

Allen closed in 1974. Ten girls graduated that last spring, bringing the total for the school's entire run to one thousand one hundred and seventy-seven.

Titus had counted eight hundred and sixty-one graduates through May 1962. More than a quarter of every woman Allen ever graduated came out of it in the final twelve years, which is another way of saying the school was killed while it was working.

No records of the school were maintained.

Not burned, not seized, not misfiled. When the doors shut, nobody kept the institutional record of what had happened in that building since 1887, and the state that had declined to educate those girls in the first place did not step in to preserve the account of who had.

In 2005 Appalachian State University funded researchers to go and find whatever was left. They recorded fifteen oral history interviews and gathered what former students and teachers still had in their own houses.

What they assembled sits now in the W. L. Eury Appalachian Collection. Two yearbooks, 1962 and 1968. Four issues of the school newspaper, from 1955 and 1956.

There are also registration brochures, concert programs, photographs and slides, a folder on the Burnsville protests during the 1959 to 1960 school year, and a run of clippings. That is the surviving paper trail of one thousand one hundred and seventy-seven women.

The project wrote in its own description that the chance to record living voices should not be missed and was quickly passing. That was written twenty-one years ago.

The alumnae had understood the problem long before the university did.

They held their first reunion in 1978, four years after the closing, and about four hundred former students were expected, among them Annis Bradshaw Pearson of the class of 1915. Afterward two of them, Margaret Johnson and Ann Woodford, wrote to the Asheville Citizen to thank the reporter who had covered it. They wanted it on the record that a landmark of Asheville would not die and be clouded in a blanket of dust.

That was forty-eight years ago.

It took until October 21, 2023, for a highway marker to go up on College Street near the register of deeds, a silver sign with black lettering that gives the school three lines. At the unveiling, one of the organizers pointed out that people in Asheville know Stephens-Lee and know the YMI, and that hardly anybody knows this. The buildings themselves are still standing, in use as offices, and one of them now houses the agency that sells the city to visitors.

The debt here is not a feeling. It is an errand with a clock on it.

If your people sat in those counties, somebody in your line may have gone down to Asheville for school, or wanted to and could not, or put money toward a niece who did. Everything anybody knows about Allen exists because women in their seventies and eighties opened boxes in 2005 for a graduate student with a recorder. The girls in that last graduating class are around seventy now, and the women who sat down with the recorder were already old when they did it.

Ask the oldest person in your family where they went to high school and who paid for it, and write the answer down while there is still somebody to answer.

Because those graduates cut and stitched the clothes they walked out in, and not one of those garments turns up anywhere in what the archive was able to gather.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXcAK
Every coffee helps me keep creating

text:
What Makes the Sabha Mandapa of the Modhera Sun Temple a Remarkable Example of Ancient Indian Architecture?

The Sabha Mandapa, also known as the Assembly Hall or Rangamandapa, is one of the most distinctive architectural features of the historic Sun Temple in Modhera, Gujarat, India. Located in Mehsana district on the left bank of the Pushpavati River, this remarkable structure reflects the artistic excellence and architectural sophistication of medieval India.

Built in the distinctive Maru-Gurjara architectural style during the Solanki period in the early eleventh century, the Sabha Mandapa is renowned for its open-pillared design, intricate stone carvings, and exceptional craftsmanship. The hall features 52 elaborately carved pillars adorned with sculptures of deities, mythological figures, and scenes associated with Hindu epics, including the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. Its carefully arranged pillars and ornate ceiling demonstrate the skill, creativity, and dedication of the artisans of that era.

Beyond its architectural beauty, the Sabha Mandapa represents an important part of Gujarat’s historical and cultural heritage. Its harmonious proportions, detailed sculptures, and sophisticated design illustrate the remarkable achievements of traditional Indian temple architecture. Today, the Modhera Sun Temple stands as a lasting testament to India's rich artistic traditions and the architectural legacy of the Solanki period.

The magnificent Sabha Mandapa of the Modhera Sun Temple reflects the artistic excellence and architectural heritage of India. Its intricate carvings, sculpted pillars, and remarkable design offer valuable insights into the artistic vision, engineering skills, and cultural traditions of ancient India.

Readers are invited to share their observations, interpretations, and appreciation of this remarkable historical monument in the comments below. Every thoughtful perspective contributes to a deeper appreciation of India's rich cultural legacy.
