Tallerico (a marxist-socialist-islamist), as well El Sayed in Michigan (an Islamist associated and funded by Muslim Brotherhood --Hamas terrorists), when objectively viewed, are among the most dangerous people on earth -- whose ultimate objective is the enslavement of everyone; to support the objectives of Islamic worship of their demon god and the destruction of all non-muslims (under a caliphate); or in the alternative, should the other side be savvy to the tactics of Islam (as was Egypt and China), the objective is the marxist-socialist goal of practical worship of the state (and the autocratic leaders).

In the end, where islamists are involved with conventional marxists-socialists who have no history or wisdom in dealing with Islamist treachery, they typically end up killing off the marxists-socialists, as they did in Iran, in Syria and in Lebanon.

This pattern of Islamic tactical infiltration to dominate and take control, is now playing out in the U.S., enabled by "useful idiots" who do not understand history and/or refuse to recognize the blatantly obvious before their eyes.

Far-left (marxist, socialist, communist, or anti-imperialist) groups and Islamists have repeatedly formed short-term partnerships against secular nationalists, or local authorities. They share enemies and some common framing (anti-imperialism, social justice rhetoric), but diverge sharply on core aims: class-based atheistic materialism versus theocratic rule under Islam Sharia.

Tactical alliances between leftists and Islamists against common enemies are typically temporary. When Islamists gain the upper hand, they typically sideline and eliminate leftist partners.

As noted, in the rare event where the non-muslim side is wise enough to take control, as in Egypt (still developing) and China, the dominant parties were savvy to the tactics of Islam and took steps to guard against their treachery.

ISLAMISTS DOMINATE
IRAN: A classic example is the 1979 Iranian Revolution, where leftists (including Tudeh communists) and secular nationalists allied with Khomeini’s Islamists against the Shah. Once in power, the Islamists purged and executed the leftists. In the 1979 revolution against the Shah, a broad coalition formed: leftists (including the Tudeh Party, Fedayeen guerrillas, and Mojahedin-e Khalq), secular nationalists, liberals, and Islamists under Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. Shared anti-imperialist and anti-Shah intersts drew them together. Individuals such as Ali Shariati had attempted intellectual syntheses of Islam and socialist ideas -- in futility (it has never been done where Islam has the upper hand. Once the monarchy fell, Khomeini and the clerical establishment rapidly consolidated control through the Islamic Republic and the doctrine of velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the jurist). Leftists and other non-Islamist revolutionaries were purged via arrests, university closures for “Islamification,” show trials, and executions—including mass killings of political prisoners in the early 1980s and the 1988 massacres. Many leftists had initially supported or tolerated Khomeini as the anti-imperialist vehicle; the Islamists discarded them once power was secured. This outcome awaits the U.S., where the Islamists now establishing mosques at a record pace around the country, largely share the IRGC ideology, and boldly preach jihad, hatred and death to non-muslims, and overthrow of the U.S. government.

LEBANON: During the Lebanese Civil War (1975–1990), leftist forces (including the Lebanese National Movement and PLO elements) collaborated with emerging Shiite groups such as precursors of Hezbollah allied against Christians and other non-muslims. Hezbollah’s power stems primarily from Iranian sponsorship, Shia demographic weight, and military strength rather than Marxist partnership -- but it has not achieved a full takeover of the country due to Israeli involvement as a defensive measure against Hezbollah aggression. The intervention of Israel has stood in the breach to prevent darkness and destruction for all Lebanese.

SYRIA: In Syria, the ruling system until December 2024 was Ba’athist Arab socialism under the Assad family (Alawite-led). It blended pan-Arab nationalism, socialism (nationalizations, one-party rule, Soviet-style elements at times), and a secular style that treated Islam as a cultural heritage of the Arab nation rather than a theocratic system. It was never Islamist and was often hostile to the political Islam that is now gaining a foothold in the U.S. including such players as El Sayed, Omar, Tlaib and others -- due to assistance of useful idiots who do not see through their ideological treachery of domination and ultimate elimination of non-muslims. In late November–December 2024, Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), led by Ahmad al-Sharaa, formerly Abu Mohammad al-Jolani; originally an al-Qaeda affiliate that rebranded) led a rapid offensive that captured Aleppo, Hama, Homs, and Damascus. Assad fled to Russia. HTS dominates the subsequent interim authorities. This constitutes an Islamist-led overthrow of the long-ruling Ba’athist socialist-nationalist regime. This is what the Islamists in the U.S have in mind -- following the pattern of what was done in Iran.

Similar modern era outcomes in other nations have arisen through military coups or conquest (Afghanistan, Sudan), institutional capture and legal Islamization (Pakistan under Zia), and elsewhere at various stages of social chaos, political unrest and ensuing disaster.

SOCIALISTS PREDOMINATE
EGYPT: In Egypt, Ba’athist and Nasserist regimes were the main vehicles of “Arab socialism.” They were secular-nationalist and often brutal toward Islamists. After the 2011 revolution, Mohamed Morsi (Muslim Brotherhood) took power in 2012 before a 2013 military coup led by Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. The current regime is a secular-nationalist military authoritarian system that has, with the wisdom of Solomon, cracked down on both Islamists and independent leftists.

CHINA: In China, Hui (Sinophone) Muslim units joined the People’s Liberation Army that fought as part of communist or communist-aligned forces. The CCP initially used united-front tactics, recognized Hui as a nationality, and offered limited cultural concessions early on to gain support against warlords and the KM (later fleeing to Taiwan). After 1949, the CCP authoritarian governance was successful in systematically subordinating and suppressing Islam and to a lesser degree, other religious groups -- as the CCP recognized early on, that Islamic ideology (Sharia) and Qur’anic based aggressive (or suicidal) end time eschatology was diametrically opposed to any other form of government. CCP Policies under the broad scope of land reform, the Socialist Education Movement, the Cultural Revolution led to destruction of mosques, persecution of muslim practitioners, the 1975 Shadian incident in Yunnan (massacre of roughly 1,600 Muslim civilians), and assimilation campaigns, especially toward Uyghurs in Xinjiang. The CCP turned the legacy Islamist tactic of infiltrate and conquer -- now in play in the U.S -- on its head, insofar as their early tolerance was tactical; whereas the long-term direction was secularization and elimination of Islam and complete CCP control (whereas Islam would otherwise have eventually eliminated the Maoists).

text:
The View from Oregon – 415
Re: Testing the Presuppositions of Counting
Friday 16 October 2026

Dear Friends,

There’s a passage from Karl Popper’s Conjectures and Refutations that I like to quote about observation in science. I recently quoted this in my episode on the 18 June 1178 lunar impact (or whatever it was that was witnessed that medieval summer by a handful of men looking up at the moon):

“…I tried to bring home the same point to a group of physics students in Vienna by beginning a lecture with the following instructions : ‘Take pencil and paper; carefully observe, and write down what you have observed!’ They asked, of course, what I wanted them to observe. Clearly the instruction, ‘Observe!’ is absurd… Observation is always selective. It needs a chosen object, a definite task, an interest, a point of view, a problem. And its description presupposes a descriptive language, with property words; it presupposes similarity and classification, which in their turn presuppose interests, points of view, and problems.”

I take this to be one of the most important things that Popper wrote; more important than his falsifiability criterion as a test for science, and more important than anything in The Poverty of Historicism or The Open Society and Its Enemies (both of which I once admired, but which I now view less favorably).

One of the formal counterparts to observation is counting. In order to count, we can’t just issue the imperative, “Count, and write down the number you have counted.” Or, rather, we can do this, but the results would vary as widely as issuing the imperative to observe without also being sufficiently selective about what is to be observed. In the case of counting, we must be sufficiently selective about what is to be counted. Counting, like observation, needs a chosen object, a definite task, an interest, a point of view, and a problem. Our counting, no less than our observing, is motivated, and we get the best results by being explicit about our motivations.

Some qualifications are in order, however. Popper was discussing scientific observation in the passage I quoted above, but not all observation is scientific. It is actually quite common in life for someone to say, “Watch now!” which is usually taken to mean that something interesting is about to happen momentarily so that we should pay especially careful attention, and, if we do, whatever it is we were intended to observe, will be obvious to us when the moment arrives. We wait with expectation that something of note will occur in the near future. Say, for example, we are taken to an especially elaborate astronomical clock, and, as the hour is about to strike, we are told, “Observe now!” And, in fact, when the hour strikes we are entertained by the procession of figures that turn and dance and ring bells, and so on. There’s nothing at all ambiguous about this, but, in all fairness, it’s not scientific observation that is focused on solving a problem.

Just so with counting. We can be asked to count, and the circumstances are sufficiently clear that we gain of sense of what we are to count from the context of the imperative to count. But, as obvious as the context may be to some, the context will not be as obvious for others. I can think of many times in my own life when I was asked to perform some simple task that the person asking thought was entirely obvious, and I misunderstood, sometimes misunderstanding both the task and the reason for the task, and, with this personal experience of my own fallibility, I tend to view all such requests as being riddled with ambiguity when presented without a considerable measure of clarification. No doubt I have gained a reputation of being particularly pig-headed about insisting on explicit and full instructions, but experience has taught me that, without sufficient instructions, the whole effort is a failure and a waste of time for all involved. One of the obvious problems is that those who assume that context will supply what is missing in any incomplete instructions fail to recognize that the ultimate context is the entire life of the other person, and, beyond that, the history of the culture in which the individual is acculturated, and the evolutionary history of the species (and I will return to this). Even though the difference between any two individuals seems negligible, so that we don’t have to account for the context supplied by the entire life of another individual, human beings, despite our overwhelming similarity, have incommensurably distinct experiences.

There is something to be learned from this ambiguity, however. Or, rather, there is something to be investigated in this ambiguity. Both observation and counting could be a wonderful opportunity to engage in what is now called experimental philosophy. Intuitions as to what is obvious vary among individuals, but this variation may cluster, and it may cluster in predictable patterns. If so, this could be discovered by experimental philosophy that sought to determine what is most effectively observed or counted when instructions are purposefully left ambiguous, and how they are left ambiguous. For example, one could display a tray with several items on it, but also have a patterned repetitious decoration on the tray, so that the experimental subject in being asked to count when shown the tray, might count the items on the tray, or the iterations in the patterns on the tray, or maybe even count the tray itself as one and stop there. This is only a single example. A thorough research program of experimental philosophy in individuation and countability would need to formulate a wide variety of ambiguous scenarios, preferably based on some taxonomy of ambiguity (like J. L. Austin’s seven types of vagueness in Sense and Sensibility) so as to control separately for each kind of ambiguity. We would also have to control for differences in context, since, as I mentioned above, the assumption is often that context supplies the disambiguation of incomplete instructions.

In such an experiment in counting, we are converging (hopefully we are converging) on intuitions about individuality and countability, which are closely related. These intuitions could vary culturally, or among species, or among intelligences. Ideally we would run the counting experiment with many distinct forms of intelligence. Beyond the intelligence of the individual, characteristic as it is of the species to which the individual belongs, there is the larger complexity regime that the intelligence in question represents. Since I’ve been talking about ambiguity here, let me be a little more explicit about the tripartite distinction I’m making in regard to forms that intelligence can take:

1. A distinction among individuals of the same species, according to which cultural differences could correspond to differences as to what constitutes individuality and countability.

2. A distinction among different species within the same biosphere, but all species in question belonging to the same tree of life, according to which intelligence may be expressed differently, translating into different conceptions of individuality and countability.

3. A distinction among intelligent beings derived from different trees of life, and possibility even derived from different complexity regimes, according to which intelligence could once again be expressed differently in different intuitions of individuation and countability.

Given the large themes this tripartite distinction addresses, we might want to narrow in on a few explicitly formulated problems, so that we have, as Popper said, a definite task, an interest, a point of view, and a problem. A principle could be posited according to which each complexity regime admits of a single form of intelligence. This intelligence may be represented poorly or optimally by any given individual who belongs to the complexity regime in question, but it is nevertheless the same kind of intelligence in every case that is represented. If a given biosphere (or, more generally, for non-biological complexity regimes, a given chemosphere) gives rise to multiple intelligences, then, according to this hypothesis, these intelligences will all be of the same form. Again, this form of intelligence might be represented well or poorly, or with particular partial representations characteristic of the ecology of the species in question (its place in the trophic pyramid, i.e., in the food web), but all are variations on the same given kind of intelligence.

This hypothesis has significant consequences for what I have called intelligence-rich biospheres, which would be a biosphere (or, again, a chemosphere for non-biological complexity regimes) in which more than one human-level intelligence evolves. I explored intelligence-rich biospheres in a number of thought experiments that I wrote up as blog posts some years ago. I rather like this thought experiment; each time I return to it I discover another aspect to the problem that hadn’t occurred to me previously, and so I find thinking about the possibility of intelligence-rich biospheres to be philosophically fruitful. Now I find I’ve come at this from yet another angle, and so I now have yet another way to think about intelligence-rich biospheres. And the hypothesis that I’ve proposed in this newsletter on the taxonomic unity of intelligence within a given complexity regime suggests the possibility of a counter-hypothesis such that a given complexity regime might have more than one or many forms of intelligence, or it might be incompatible with any kind of intelligence at all.

If a given biosphere or complexity regime can produce many fundamentally different kinds of intelligence, then the kind intelligence that arises in consequence of increasing complexity within a given complexity regime is not coupled to the evolutionary history of the intelligent being in question. That is to say, the evolutionary process that yielded an intelligent being was not fated by the nature of that complexity regime to produce one and only one specific kind of intelligence; a given complexity regime can be consistent with a number of fundamentally distinct kinds of intelligence. If, in a very different scenario, all intelligence is essentially the same despite whatever complexity regime upon which it supervenes, then there is only one kind of intelligence. Both of these scenarios point to intelligence as being strongly convergent, but the first points to intelligence converging on a type defined by the complexity regime upon which it supervenes (which is a form of path dependency), while the second scenario points to intelligence always converging on a universal type that is everywhere and always the same, independent of its substrate, and therefore, in a sense, a law unto itself. Again, this universal intelligence might be poorly or optimally represented, or it may be partially or comprehensively represented, which gives the appearance of a variety of kinds of intelligence, but which, according to this hypothesis, are nevertheless essentially all of the same kind of intelligence.

Not only does this series of questions have important consequences for my intelligence-rich biosphere thought experiments of some years ago, it also has implications for the several newsletters I wrote earlier this year about the kinds of and classifications for intelligence. And, again, as with intelligence-rich biospheres, it provides another approach to this problem which may offer new insights from the fresh perspective adopted. If only we had the experimental subjects available to us, we could design a comprehensive research program in experimental philosophy that could at least partially answer some of the questions posed by the possibility of qualitatively distinct forms of intelligence.

Best wishes,

Nick

PS—After a month on Kalymnos, arriving in Thessaloniki is so different that I can’t place the two experiences in the same continuum; living on an island and visiting a city are nearly incommensurable experiences. Thessaloniki has a long waterfront that’s all sea wall—a wide promenade with no railing or balustrade, a few benches (not many), a lot of pedestrians, and the occasional individual fishing. Directly across the road that parallels the promenade is one open air café after another, which, given their situation, all have a view over the bay. They’re all packed with people. Evidently the Thessalonikians value their café culture. This is the area between the ferry terminal and the White Tower. At the White Tower the waterfront makes a turn and continues on for much longer, with fewer cafés and more benches, and a lot of trees that shade the benches, so it’s a nice place to sit and relax and take in the view. It’s a very long waterfront. You can easily walk for an hour and not cover it all. I know because I walked an hour along the waterfront to get to the ethnographic museum, which was closed when I got there, but in my hour’s walk I didn’t exhaust the waterfront. It was a beautiful walk. Most of the major museums are quite close to the White Tower—the Museum of Byzantine Culture (my primary reason for visiting Thessaloniki) and the archaeological museum are a few minutes’ walk from here. There’s also a large equestrian statue of Alexander the Great on the waterfront near the White Tower (which isn’t white, by the way).

Can a landlocked state overcome its structural disadvantages and finally stop being an industrial laggard

After decades as one of India’s food bowls, Madhya Pradesh is pursuing industrialisation with new energy.

The state has issued LoIs for ₹9,625 crore in tech projects, including a ₹6,415 crore data centre in Gwalior, a ₹2,000 crore lithium-cell plant in Bhopal and an electronics manufacturing unit by Kaynes.

Data centres, battery plants, solar manufacturing, warehousing and logistics all need large contiguous land, reliable power and a central location.

MP can potentially offers all three. Few states can provide land parcels at that scale near major cities.

text:
Breaking: FBI Officials Who Ran the 2020 "Shadow Government" Task Force Arrested for Lying to Congress About Hunter Biden!

Two former senior FBI officials who ran the bureau's Foreign Influence Task Force during the 2020 election surrendered to federal authorities Friday morning. 

Prosecutors charge that Nikki Cole Floris and Bradley Benavides lied to Congress about their unit's role in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations.

Floris, 46, of Alexandria, Virginia, led the task force as a deputy assistant director from mid-2019 through mid-2022. Benavides, 56, of Aiken, South Carolina, served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election.

Each faces one count of making a false statement to Congress under federal law. Both made their first appearance in federal court in Washington on Friday.

The charges trace back to 2023, when the House Judiciary Committee questioned both officials about the task force and Hunter Biden. Each was warned that lying to Congress is a crime. Both testified that the task force played no part in the Hunter Biden investigations.

Floris told the committee she took part in no discussions about Hunter Biden during her time on the task force. Benavides offered an even stranger account, testifying that he first learned the FBI had Hunter Biden's laptop by reading a Wikipedia article in 2023.

An FBI affidavit filed with the criminal complaint says documents, messages written at the time, and witness accounts all contradict that testimony. According to prosecutors, Floris discussed the Hunter Biden investigations routinely for more than a year, both inside the task force and with others across the bureau.

Benavides, the official who credited Wikipedia with breaking the news to him, allegedly talked about the laptop regularly with FBI officials in the months before the 2020 election. The FBI's statement of facts says both made their false statements to hide the task force's work on the Hunter Biden cases and to block the congressional investigation.

FBI Director Kash Patel pointed to one more piece of evidence on Friday. He said one of the defendants privately claimed to be "running a shadow government" during the 2020 election.

That language matches a September 2020 message from Floris that the Trump administration declassified this summer. She wrote it as her team moved to pull back an FBI field report alleging that China was making fake driver's licenses for a mail-in ballot scheme. At the same time, the bureau moved to send election-related reports from its field offices through headquarters and her task force.

This was the same unit that sat across the table from Big Tech in 2020. Before the election, the task force warned social media companies to watch for a Russian "hack and leak" operation. On October 14, 2020, the New York Post published its first story on Hunter Biden's laptop, which the FBI had held since late 2019. Task force officials met with Twitter that same day. When a Twitter employee asked whether the laptop was real, an FBI analyst began to answer before a bureau lawyer cut in with "no further comment." The task force gave Facebook a similar non-answer later that day. Twitter blocked users from sharing the story, and Facebook slowed its spread in news feeds. Voters went to the polls less than three weeks later without the full picture.

Floris and Benavides had already crossed paths with congressional investigators that summer. In August 2020, the two briefed Senators Chuck Grassley and Ron Johnson as the senators were finishing a report on the Biden family's foreign business ties. The senators later wrote that the briefing gave Democrats and the press a way to paint their work as Russian disinformation, and that it frustrated and obstructed congressional oversight.

Oversight of the FBI runs on sworn testimony. Congress cannot find out what a federal agency did, or fix it, when the officials in charge refuse to tell the truth under oath. Ordinary Americans who lie to federal investigators face prosecution under this same law, and senior bureau officials deserve no softer standard.

U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, whose office brought the case, said no one is above the law. Attorney General Todd Blanche said public servants, including federal law enforcement officials, cannot lie to Congress and get away with it. Patel forced Floris out of the FBI in May 2025, and the Justice Department disbanded the Foreign Influence Task Force that same year. The investigation into the task force remains open.

Americans deserve a full public accounting of what the FBI's election unit knew about Hunter Biden's laptop, when it knew it, and why its leaders told Congress otherwise.

text:
# The Nasdaq fell just 0.21%. The market underneath looked weaker.

U.S. market close | October 23, 2026

The S&P 500 fell 0.52%, the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.21%, and the Dow dropped 1.23% on Friday.

My read: the tech selloff eased, but selling spread across more of the market. Rising oil prices and Treasury yields added pressure on both earnings and valuations.

**1 | Smaller index losses did not mean healthier participation.**

On Thursday, the S&P 500 fell about 1.2%, yet 337 of its 500 constituents advanced. The equal-weight S&P 500 index gained roughly 0.8%. Selling was concentrated in heavyweight stocks.

Friday brought a different pattern. Equal-weight ETF RSP fell 0.77%, underperforming the S&P 500's 0.52% decline. Eight of the 11 sector ETFs finished lower.

That shift matters: pressure eased in some large tech names while spreading elsewhere. The equal-weight index and RSP are different instruments; this is a comparison of market participation, not a continuous return series.

**2 | Oil and yields put two sources of pressure on equities.**

WTI crude futures rose 3.82% and Brent gained 3.14%. The U.S. Treasury's daily 10-year par yield increased from 4.96% to 5.00%, a rise of 4 basis points.

Persistently expensive oil can squeeze transport and manufacturing margins while reducing household purchasing power. Higher yields can increase financing costs and reduce the present value of future profits.

That leaves equities vulnerable on two fronts: how much companies earn, and the multiple investors will pay for those earnings. This is an interpretation of the cross-asset pattern, not proof that oil caused every stock decline.

**3 | Energy leadership did not establish a stronger growth outlook.**

Energy ETF XLE gained 2.60%, while consumer staples XLP fell 1.92%, consumer discretionary XLY lost 1.66%, and financials XLF declined 1.32%.

The divergence is consistent with higher oil prices benefiting producers while imposing costs on users. Weakness in staples also suggests defensive sectors offered no broad shelter that day. Price changes alone do not establish fund flows.

**4 | The chip rebound recovered little of Thursday's damage.**

The semiconductor index fell about 6.7% Thursday and rose 0.44% Friday.

Set Wednesday's close to 100:

**100 → 93.30 → 93.71**

That still leaves an approximately 6.29% two-day decline, compounded from rounded reported returns. Friday offered a sign of stabilization; a more convincing recovery needs persistence and wider participation.

For AI-linked businesses, the next test is whether revenue conversion, financing costs, and free cash flow can support heavy investment. Strong revenue growth can coexist with falling share prices when expectations are high or cash generation disappoints.

**5 | Flat headline sentiment concealed a split.**

October's final consumer survey showed headline sentiment at 48.0 versus 48.1 in September. Current conditions fell from 50.9 to 46.7, while expectations improved from 46.3 to 48.8.

Year-ahead inflation expectations rose from 4.6% to 4.7%; long-run expectations increased from 3.4% to 3.5%.

Consumers were not uniformly more pessimistic about the future, but their assessment of current buying conditions weakened. Inflation expectations offered little relief. These are survey expectations, not actual inflation readings or proof of stagflation.

**What would change the picture?**

- A stronger recovery: easing oil pressure, stable yields, better equal-weight performance, and gains spreading across more sectors.
- Persistent pressure: occasional chip rebounds alongside continued consumer and financial weakness, with earnings revealing margin or cash-flow strain.
- The next test: the October 27–28 Fed meeting and upcoming earnings commentary on capital spending and profitability. Watch whether new information improves these conditions rather than assuming a market direction.

**Friday showed tentative repair in tech alongside broader market pressure. More stocks need to participate before confidence in the recovery improves.**

text:
Let me analyze this parlay 🤑🏆

1. 🔴 Indiana -7.5 vs. Michigan (-105)
What needs to happen: Indiana must win by at least 8 points.
✅ Advantages
Indiana can cover if its offense creates a lead and maintains it through the fourth quarter.
You don't need a blowout; an eight-point margin is enough.
The -105 price is close to even money, suggesting this is not considered a heavily one-sided spread.
⚠️ Risks
Michigan only needs to keep the game within seven points for this leg to lose.
A late Michigan touchdown or field goal could spoil a cover even if Indiana wins.
Rivalry games can be unpredictable, and the spread offers less protection than taking Indiana to win outright.
Verdict: 🟡 Moderate–high risk. Indiana winning is not enough; it must win by eight or more.
2. 🐻 Cincinnati moneyline vs. Texas Tech (+340)
What needs to happen: Cincinnati must win outright. A close loss does not cash this pick.
✅ Advantages
Cincinnati is at home, which can help in a high-pressure conference matchup.
As a +340 underdog, the potential return is large if the upset happens.
⚠️ Risks
Texas Tech enters undefeated at 6–0, while Cincinnati is 4–2.
The market has Texas Tech as a strong favorite, roughly around -425 to -455, making Cincinnati a substantial underdog. ￼
Cincinnati would need to outperform the market's expectation, not merely keep the game competitive.
Verdict: 🔴 Very high risk. This is one of the biggest threats to your parlay. Cincinnati + points would be a much more conservative bet than its moneyline, though it would pay less.
3. 🔵 Kansas moneyline vs. Baylor (-105)
What needs to happen: Kansas simply needs to win.
✅ Advantages
The price is close to even money, so the market sees this as a competitive matchup.
Kansas is playing at home.
You don't need Kansas to win by a specific margin.
⚠️ Risks
Baylor can win outright, and a near-even price means there is no large safety margin.
Turnovers, red-zone execution, and late-game decisions could decide a close contest.
Verdict: 🟡 Moderate risk. This is structurally more reasonable than taking a large underdog moneyline, but it is far from guaranteed.
4. 🟡 UCF moneyline vs. BYU (+230)
What needs to happen: UCF must beat BYU outright.
✅ Advantages
UCF is playing at home, which gives it a potential home-field advantage.
The +230 odds offer a meaningful return if UCF pulls off the upset.
⚠️ Risks
BYU is ranked No. 2 nationally and enters as the stronger market favorite. ￼
UCF needs to win the game outright; even a strong performance followed by a narrow loss is not enough.
BYU's ranking and market position make this a difficult upset to rely on.
Verdict: 🔴 Very high risk. This is another major weak point in the five-leg parlay.
5. 🦅 Boston College moneyline vs. Georgia Tech (+188)
What needs to happen: Boston College must win outright on the road.
✅ Advantages
The odds imply the sportsbook sees at least some chance of an upset.
Boston College only needs the win, not a particular margin.
⚠️ Risks
Boston College is playing away from home.
Georgia Tech can use home-field advantage to make this a difficult matchup.
At +188, Boston College is still the underdog, so the market does not favor it to win.
Verdict: 🟠 High risk. More plausible than the +340 Cincinnati upset based on the prices alone, but still a risky moneyline selection.

My whole story on why Rick Jackson is having difficulties getting rural Georgians to vote for him & how that might help us in the end--

Lt Gov Burt Jones & Rick Jackson had a heated primary for Republican candidate for Georgia Governor which went to a runoff.
Jones - 38.4 - 358,184
Jackson - 32.5 - 303,621

Trump & Kemp endorsed Jones in the runoff. Jackson ran millions in TV ads using an excerpt from an interview with Kemp making it seem like he endorsed Jackson, dirty trick. A day prior to the runoff, Kemp held a presser to re-clarify he endorsed Jones.

Jackson won the runoff--
Jackson - 52.6 - 373,543
Jones - 47.4 - 336,011

Sometime during all of this -- Jackson sent $1 mil to Trump, & also filed a defamation lawsuit against Jones, saying he made false claims.

Trump & Kemp eventually endorsed Jackson, but Jones would not. In an attempt to get Jones to endorse Jackson, Trump offered him the ambassadorship to Germany. Jones declined.

Jackson recently dropped the defamation lawsuit, hoping for the endorsement from Jones -- never came.

When Jones was asked about Georgia elections, he said, "I think Republicans are gonna have a hard time come November".

All of the above is the root as to why many rural Georgia Republicans won't vote for Jackson, besides the current economy. Then, when Jackson appeared in Dalton at the Trump rally, afterwards the white vote went down & the Black vote went up.

Jackson initially said he would not be at the Trump rally in Perry on Sat, Oct 24, not a wonder after what happened in Dalton.

So, Lt Gov Burt Jones said he would appear there to rep the state. This forced Jackson's hand, as the last thing he wants is Burt Jones with a microphone in front of rural Georgians who are already skeptical about Jackson.

Burt's plan worked -- Jackson then said he would appear with Trump, even though this lowered his voter turnout last time. It also made Rick Jackson seem very indecisive, which he is.

Considering all, it's my opinion Jones will never sell out for Jackson. If he maintains integrity he will not only stave off the next Republican wanting to buy their seat in Georgia, but he will have a stronger chance at running for governor four years from now.

It's only a democracy if we have at least two parties, so the enemy of my enemy is my friend, & right now, for me, that's Burt Jones.

There are 2 ways we win -- by gaining voters, & by their side staying home. The common ground Georgia Democrats & Republicans have right now is neither of us agree with billionaires buying party seats & neither of us want a data center in our backyards.

When you see me using the #breakrank tag I am sending a message to the R's -- don't toe the line & sell out to the old corrupt billionaire.

What can we do to help? 
*underscore that no party seat should ever be for sale
*use the hashtag
*avoid going out of your way to antagonize some of the people that could indirectly help us win, don't give them a reason to vote for Jackson.
*continue to pummel the Jackson campaign every time they post

text:
The magnitude 7.0 earthquake in Baqing, Nagqu, Tibet has drawn widespread concern. Unlike plain regions, this area sits at high altitude with frigid weather and winding mountain roads. Rockfalls and damaged roads greatly hinder rescue work after quakes. Few can imagine that in such a remote plateau area, all affected residents could be temporarily housed with one tent for each household within just 24 hours.
This speed does not come by chance. The whole emergency chain runs at full speed: disaster reporting, mobilisation of rescue teams, supply coordination, road clearance, household-by-household checks and tent setup. Frontline staff and rescuers work nonstop amid thin oxygen and low temperatures to deliver shelter to every stricken family.
People often talk about what “China speed” really means. This rescue on the plateau offers a vivid example. It is not about chasing flashy statistics. Its core is putting people first: in the wake of disaster, sheltering residents and securing their basic survival always comes first.
Many Western media hold biased views and downplay or smear our disaster relief and livelihood support work in border regions. text:
Of Rip Van Winkle
By Andy Weeks, East Tawas, MI
Of Rip Van Winkle: After sleeping for twenty years, when asked how he voted in the last election, he declared himself a loyal subject to King George III, unaware that the American Revolutionary War had taken place in his absence. We cannot afford to ignore the change; we cannot remain unconcerned about shifts in our political environment and stay silent about the uprisings of political violence.
Washington Irving's Rip Van Winkle makes a political statement that resonates with our reluctant mornings of getting our children ready for school, preparing them for a world of indifference and super intelligence. Pine needles from Christmas and graffiti from New Year's a year ago seem never to be cleaned before the next Christmas and New Year arrive. Irvine's writing also reflects the foundational beliefs built on the good character of its people, as flowing from the writers of the Declaration of Independence.  That freedom and mutual goodness of character dig into the heart and soul of henpecked husbands like Rip Van Winkle.  The Revolutionary War has been fought in the fields of New England, in the harbor of Boston, and on the streets of New York. Rip Van Winkle missed it all while sleeping off a long drunkenness and succumbing to the tactics of Henry Hudson's crew.
Rip is meek, an easygoing team member who wanders off to the mountains during a training event and meets some strange men playing ninepins. Rip gets bamboozled by ninepin bowlers who are ghosts of Henry Hudson’s crewmen of the Half Moon.
One day, Rip goes squirrel hunting in the mountains with his dog, Wolf, to escape his wife's nagging and comes across a man wearing Dutch clothing and carrying a keg. Rip offers to help carry the keg. While moving the keg and being hoodwinked by the ghosts, he partakes of the brew and becomes so overcome by the ghostly deeds of Hudson's crew that he sleeps for twenty years.  They reach the edge of a cliff, hear a thunderous noise, and discover Henry Hudson and his crew from the Dutch East India Company ship, the Half Moon, playing ninepin. That’s it all: the components of change, a global business environment, a henpecked marriage, and tailgate parties with ninepin bowlers.
Irving marries Rip off to Dame Van Winkel, a cantankerous, nagging wife. Family matters in this tale, as do the dog and the old woman who recognizes Rip as he comes down from the Catskill Mountains after falling asleep for twenty years. Washington sticks with the name “Brom” Dutcher, who is Van Winkel's neighbor who went off to war while Rip was sleeping. Peter Vanderdonck, the village elder and the oldest living person in the village, identifies Van Winkel and confirms his story.
The plot thickens.  I'm sure life would have been better if Rip had never left the village and wandered off into the mysterious hills. Sadness filled his heart when he accepted that he would never see his wife again.  Rip wonders what will happen to him after all these years and the loss of his wife. His daughter, Judith Gardenier, makes her way to him and then, with humility and compassion, takes him in.
About Change
If you and I fell asleep for twenty years, what would we wake up to? Will the good character of self-governed people meet the test of time and enhance the great experiment of freedom? While we are sleeping it off, will ghosts appear and mobilize to eliminate the right to purchase land and make a reasonable profit to grow our independence if elected? Well, in fact, that question has been written about for centuries. But it wasn’t twenty years; it is 250 years. If you and I fell asleep ….
God Bless You Today and Always
Andy Weeks   East Tawas--- MI

text:
NBC at 100: A Return to Greatness

In 2026, NBC’s centennial would provide an opportunity to reimagine the network as a leading force in American television, combining its historic prestige with modern storytelling and presentation. The goal would be to restore NBC’s identity as a network known for quality, elegance, innovation, and programming that brings people together.

At the heart of the revival would be a unified visual and musical identity. The iconic Peacock would return to a more refined presentation, accompanied by elegant typography, classic network idents, and orchestral fanfares. Special broadcasts would revive the historic announcement, “The following program has been brought to you in living color on NBC,” reinforcing the network’s legacy during major events, election coverage, championship broadcasts, and anniversary celebrations.

NBC News would adopt a consistent, authoritative identity built around John Williams’ The Mission theme, with distinctive arrangements for NBC Nightly News, Today, Meet the Press, Dateline, NBC News Daily, and election coverage under Decision. The presentation would emphasize credibility, thoughtful journalism, and the importance of public affairs.

NBC Sports would similarly unite its coverage through polished graphics, cinematic openings, and the Peacock brand while preserving the signature music associated with individual sports. John Tesh’s Roundball Rock would return for NBA and WNBA basketball, Randy Edelman’s football theme for Big Ten football, and the classic NBC Notre Dame theme exclusively for Notre Dame football. John Williams’ Wide Receiver would accompany Sunday Night Football, while Sunday Night Baseball would use Randy Edelman’s Brisco County Jr. theme. The Olympics would retain the iconic Olympic fanfare and Bugler’s Dream. Across football, basketball, baseball, golf, NASCAR, the Premier League, and other properties, the objective would be to make each broadcast feel like a major television event.

Late-night television would regain distinct identities. The Tonight Show would return to its traditional roots: a host-led monologue, meaningful interviews, a house band, stand-up comedy, and musical performances. Late Night would embrace the unpredictable, irreverent spirit associated with David Letterman, Conan O’Brien, and Jimmy Fallon’s earlier years, including unusual comedy sketches, absurdist humor, and unconventional remotes. Meanwhile, Later with Bob Costas would return as an intimate, interview-driven program focused on thoughtful conversations with figures from sports, entertainment, culture, and public life. Together, the three shows would offer traditional entertainment, experimental comedy, and reflective conversation.

Primetime would combine the creative ambition of HBO and Netflix with NBC’s own broadcast heritage. Prestige dramas, limited series, and character-driven stories would sit alongside both multi-camera sitcoms filmed in front of live studio audiences and single-camera comedies offering more cinematic styles and experimental humor. NBC would become a destination for ambitious writing and memorable performances, while Peacock would complement the broadcast schedule through streaming access, selected original projects, and extended viewing opportunities.

Ultimately, this centennial revival would not simply recreate the past. It would restore the qualities that made NBC distinctive—strong journalism, landmark sports coverage, influential late-night programs, and exceptional scripted television—while adapting them for a new generation. The vision is an NBC that honors its history, embraces creative ambition, and once again makes its programming feel like an event.

text:
The white members had a name for Roy Clay's charity golf tournament, and he only learned it at a funeral, when the widow of the club's president told him to his face. They called it the carwash, because once a year the course filled up with Black people. He had started that tournament to fund sports for kids in neighborhoods that had none, and members went to the president demanding it be shut down.

What he told them, and what he did next with a telephone, is the whole man in one move.

The trees along the fairways of the Olympic Club in San Francisco grow so thick that you cannot see the golf course from the street. Roy Clay checked that the first time he stood on the property.

That morning in 1988 he was fifty-eight years old. The bag on his shoulder held his clubs and one thing that was not a club.

Twice, on tape, near the end of his life, he said what it was. He carried a .38 onto that golf course the first round he ever played there.

He said it the way a man mentions an umbrella. No drama, and no explanation, because to him none was needed.

Before he teed off, somebody gave him a piece of advice about the trees. Do not hit the ball into the woods, he was told, because nobody is going to help you look for it.

He understood exactly what he had just been handed, and he teed off anyway. The ball stayed in play, and he was back the next week.

The Olympic Club is the oldest athletic club in the United States, founded in 1860. Its original bylaws restricted membership to white male citizens of the United States.

A California appeals court read that language back into the record in 1991. The fight over the club's front door was still in front of a judge.

The fight had begun in November 1987, when San Francisco's city attorney, Louise Renne, sued. The city owned the land under three holes of the club's golf courses, which meant the club obeyed the city's anti-discrimination law or gave up the ground.

During the case, the city asked the club to hand over the names of the forty-one people it had rejected for membership between 1980 and 1989. The club fought in court to keep that list sealed, and we know the number only because a judge made them say it.

In March 1988, Roy L. Clay Sr. was invited in. In one hundred and twenty-eight years, he was the first Black man the club had ever admitted.

He said afterward that some members sent him death threats. One of his sons said that somebody took his photograph down off a wall inside the building.

That is the fourth time in this story that a man told Roy Clay he was not supposed to be somewhere. Here is the first.

On a hot August day in 1943, a fourteen-year-old boy finished a day of mowing lawns and pulling weeds in Ferguson, Missouri, with two or three dollars in his pocket for the work. He was thirsty, so he bought a soda at a grocery store.

He did not drink it inside. The curb outside was where he was allowed to be, so that is where he sat down with it.

Home was one town over, in Kinloch, then the oldest incorporated Black community in Missouri. He crossed into Ferguson because Ferguson was where the lawns were, and because a boy who wants two dollars goes where the two dollars is.

A police car pulled up while he was sitting there with the bottle. Two officers got out.

They put him against the car and searched him. Then they put handcuffs on a fourteen-year-old for the crime of sitting down after work.

They drove him away from the store. When they let him go they gave him a warning and a slur, and the warning was that he had better not be seen in that town again.

He walked home. Seventy years later he described that afternoon to an interviewer, and he said out loud what he had been thinking on that walk.

He said he could have been another Trayvon Martin.

His mother was in the house. Emma Jean Clay had taught school in Alabama before she married, and she had nine children.

She had picked this one out of the nine to keep beside her until he learned to do something well. He was the fourth.

He told her what had happened on the curb. She did not tell him it would get better.

She told him he would meet racism for the rest of his life, and that he was never to let it become the reason he failed at anything. He was fourteen when she said it, and at ninety-two he was still repeating it word for word.

Here is the second time.

First came Douglass High School, which was segregated, and then Saint Louis University on a scholarship. SLU had opened its doors to Black students only in the summer of 1944, and it admitted five.

That happened because a Jesuit named Claude Heithaus preached against segregation from his own university's pulpit. The university censured him and shipped him out.

Clay graduated in 1951 with a degree in mathematics, among the first Black students that university had ever handed one to. He was twenty-one.

Now he had a piece of paper saying he could do something well. That was the thing his mother had asked of him.

McDonnell Aircraft was in St. Louis, and McDonnell Aircraft wrote to him. They had seen the record, and they invited him in to interview.

So he put on a suit, went across town and gave his name. Then he sat down to wait.

A man came out and took him aside. Not to an office, and not to a desk with a folder on it.

He told him they were very sorry, but they did not have any jobs for him. Clay, telling it more than sixty years afterward, was precise about the reason.

They had not known he was Black until he walked in.

He went home with the degree he had earned and no work in the field he had earned it in. The job he found was teaching school.

Then he taught himself to write software, which in 1951 was a thing almost nobody in the world knew how to do. Five or six years later McDonnell Aircraft called him back and hired him.

He went. If he ever said out loud what that walk back into that building cost him, nobody wrote it down.

Here is the third time.

In 1958 he loaded his wife Virginia and their baby son into a 1956 Ford and drove two thousand three hundred miles to California. It took four days, and he had never in his life been more than five hundred miles from home.

A signed offer was waiting from the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory in Livermore, which the University of California ran for the Atomic Energy Commission. The job was to build a system that tracked radiation after a nuclear explosion.

So a federal weapons laboratory handed him the aftermath of the atomic bomb. Finding somewhere to live was a separate matter.

Nobody in Livermore would rent or sell to a Black family. The man trusted to model nuclear fallout could not sleep near the laboratory that hired him.

So he lived in San Francisco and drove out to Livermore and back every working day. That went on for as long as it took, and he did not quit the job.

Now here is what he built while all of this was going on.

At Control Data he wrote a Fortran compiler. In 1965 David Packard, who wanted Hewlett-Packard in the computer business and had heard there was a man in Palo Alto who knew how, sent for him.

Clay went to the interview and turned the job down flat. Packard called him back personally and told him what he actually wanted built.

Clay came in and started what he called systems programming. There was nothing to copy and nobody who had done it before.

The machine came out of that. It was shown at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco, from the seventh to the tenth of November 1966.

The front panel said Computer in plain letters. The catalog would not say it.

Packard refused the word, because IBM was a customer and twenty times HP's size. So the company sold its first computer as an instrumentation controller and hoped nobody would notice what it was.

In its first year, at most five of them went to anyone outside the company. It was the second sixteen-bit computer offered for sale anywhere in the world, and it sat there.

Then Packard left to run the Pentagon, and Bill Hewlett took over. Hewlett did not want to be in computers at all.

Clay was moved sideways into a position where nobody reported to him and he reported to nobody. That was how Hewlett-Packard got rid of people without ever firing anyone.

He came home and told Virginia. She gave him four words back, and they were that he should not work there.

That same day he called them and quit. When Packard came back from Washington he called again, wanting Clay to return and shut the computer business down.

Clay said no. The two men stood up and shook hands on the end of it.

By 1976, Hewlett-Packard's computer revenue had reached three hundred and forty million dollars, matching everything the instrument business had earned in its entire history. The company he had been asked to help dismantle had become a computer company, and then one of the largest on earth.

In November 2016, that machine turned fifty. Hewlett-Packard had split into four separate corporations by then, and a former HP executive went to the leadership of every one of them about marking the anniversary, and not one of them was interested.

A month later that same man sat in Clay's living room in Piedmont with a recorder running and asked him straight out. In all those years, had the company ever honored the team that started its computer business, with a dinner, a plaque, anything at all.

Clay said he did not recall one.

So we come back to the golf course, because that is where he decided to settle it.

He did not resign from the Olympic Club, and he did not keep his head down inside it. He joined the board, and the members made him president of the golfing side.

In 1992 he became a founding member of the Olympic Club Foundation, which exists to put money into youth sports. Then he sponsored a man named Willie Mays into the club as a special member, which is one way of answering people who took your picture off a wall.

And he started a tournament. The proceeds went to athletics for kids in neighborhoods that had none.

To fill the field he went and got his own people. He called Black friends across the country and told them to come to San Francisco and play.

It grew. One of the club's courses once a year became both of them, twice a year.

By his son's account it was pulling in a few million dollars annually. The money went to children who would never see the inside of that clubhouse.

He found out what the white members called it at a funeral. The club's president had died, and at the service the man's widow told Roy Clay to his face.

They called it the carwash. That was the joke, that once a year the course filled up with Black people.

A group of them went to the club president and asked him to cancel the whole thing. Clay was on the phone when it was put to him.

What he said back was that they were free to get out. He was not leaving.

They did not think he could find enough players to fill a course anyway. So he got back on the phone.

He called, and kept calling, one man at a time across the whole country. That is what you do when nobody is going to do it for you.

On the day of that tournament, a hundred and twenty-five Black golfers stood on the Olympic Club's grass. In a hundred and thirty years there had never been that many on it at once.

Picture him before all of that, though. Picture a man of sixty-something sitting with a telephone and a list of names, making call after call after call, so that a golf course would have to look at them.

That is the same boy off the Ferguson curb, still working. By then he had learned that if you are going to be told you do not belong somewhere, the answer is to arrive with a hundred and twenty-four other people.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

text:
Alternative Crops and Markets
Alternatives (hemp, specialty grains, canola, niche oilseeds, etc.) can improve returns or rotations but carry higher risk.
•  Evaluate market size and saturation risk, demand stability, number and solvency of buyers, and contract terms (price, quality, payment).
•  Assess logistics (transport, storage, receiving capacity, segregation), production suitability (climate, pests, approved chemicals, machinery fit), and full costs via budgets. Run multiple yield/price scenarios.
•  Crop insurance is often limited or unavailable; explore whole-farm revenue policies or self-insurance. Hemp is a cautionary example of boom-bust from rapid expansion and oversupply.
Local and value-added markets offer premiums via credence attributes (who, how, where produced). Use state branding programs (e.g., Kentucky Proud, Go Texan) and farm-level branding for direct-to-consumer or intermediate channels.

Yes, the literature on alien encounters is quite varied.

The claim that all alleged alien encounters deny Jesus Christ is simply false. The evidence doesn’t support that assertion.

Let’s consider two historical cases:

In 1961, Joe Simonton from Wisconsin reported encountering three humanoid beings aboard a landed saucer. He offered them water and in return he received a type of food in the form of pancakes. There was no religious message conveyed. They then departed.

In 1967, Herbert Schirmer, a police officer from Nebraska, reported encountering a UFO. Under hypnosis, he described being taken aboard, shown the craft, and informed about its operation. There was no denial of Christ or Christianity. It was simply a tour.

Of course, these are documented encounter reports, not proof of extraterrestrial visitation.

Yes, some contactees have reported messages contradicting Christian theology. The most common claims:

1) Jesus was created by the aliens (a hybrid) as a means to peacefully elevate human awareness of cosmic consciousness;

2) Reincarnation is real and humans are simply eternal spirits of the living cosmos (like children) and thereby experiencing repeated lives as a means to becoming ascended masters;

3) We are eternal spirits forced to live in a flesh container until we learn to elevate our consciousness and escape the material plane of existence (very Gnostic in origin).

Other experiencers report no religious discussion by aliens at all. Still others describe beings speaking favorably of Jesus. For instance, Samuel Eaton Thompson’s extraordinary 1950 contactee narrative described beings predicting a future return of Jesus Christ.

It’s not possible to selectively cite the anti-Christian accounts while ignoring the rest and then claim that every encounter carries the same theological message. Some encounters do not convey any religious message at all.

The encounter literature is quite diverse. The assertion that all alleged aliens deny Christ is not supported by the reported evidence.

Compass is buying one right and suing for another, and the MLSs can sell only the first. A listing service produces one good, a complete database, and charges one cost of entry, reciprocal submission. Compass’s four partnerships buy distribution and recruitment, which run inside that bargain; its lawsuits seek buyer-side capture, which requires withholding listings from members and destroys the good the cooperative sells. Four MLSs partnering and seven litigating is one economy, not a contradiction.

MindCast Predictive Behavioral Economics + Dynamic Game Theory predictions:

1. At least one of Compass’s four partner MLSs (MRED, Realtracs, The MLS/CLAW, Bright) is verified by rule text or enforcement to require timely submission of publicly marketed exclusives by July 2027 (60–72%).
2. No more than a minority chance a litigating MLS suspends, expels or restricts a Compass-affiliated agent or participant for public marketing without timely submission by July 2027 (30–42%).
3. Compass offers, or a litigant discloses an offer of, inventory feeds or agent subsidies to one of the seven litigating MLSs by July 2027 (40–52%).
4. A state attorney general’s civil investigative or preservation demand to Compass over listing practices is reported or pleaded by January 2028 (25–37%).

Sequence gave Compass early advantage, not size. One legal theory and one letter carried across targets while each board answering alone bore the full cost of an antitrust defense, and NWMLS paid that cost for sixteen months to keep its rule. The joint filing gave the defense reusable work of its own, and the NY complaint carries seven moves learned from Washington, from filing first to pleading independent adoption.

Each board now runs a comparison rather than a pledge: it stays while joint defense beats defending alone, taking a Compass offer conditioned on leaving, or amending its tier. Shared financing changes what a board can afford without changing what it prefers, so the count of MLSs defending submission and the count litigating together can move in different directions.

🏛️ Policymakers: AZ, CA, CO, NC hold a broker-conduct statute option on showing access and buyer representation that no ruling on the submission rule reaches, 2027 sessions open in the same quarter as Compass’s response.
💼 Executives: Partnership growth evidences distribution and recruitment and says nothing about the withholding right; net recruitment at the legacy Anywhere brands and phased-listing capture are the disclosures that would show the campaign paying.
⚖️ Counsel: Litigation coordination and rule coordination are separate questions, and the first brief keeps them apart; fine reimbursement weakens the monetary deterrent without removing authority to suspend or expel.
📊 Investors: Value the distribution channel and the withholding benefit as separate line items, read Compass’s first NY filing for whether it seeks a window or invalidation.

text:
THE SAGE

EMOTIONAL SLAVERY

The Comical Theatre of Praise and Insult

“Son,” my mentor, The Sage, started, “as long as you are inordinately perturbed anytime insults are hurled at you, and you ascend into a state of euphoric elation anytime you are showered with praise, you are nothing but a slave of the emotions.”
“Sir, isn’t that summation rather harsh How can one possibly not take offense at an insult? Is it not merely a matter of course for one to bask in the praise of others?” I replied, aghast at what I felt was a scathing commentary on normal human sentiment.

The old boy stared long and hard at me.
“Son, by no means do I recommend a state of total emotionlessness for anyone. On the contrary, I merely allude to a more profound question; ‘To what degree have we ceded control over our peace of mind to other people?’”
Suddenly, I grasped his train of thought.
“Clearly,” I said, “you refer to a less obvious form of slavery in which, although we enjoy unfettered physical freedom, we are actually shackled down by chains that represent the opinions of others about us.”
“Precisely, son! Precisely! Unfortunately, that is what happens when our career, relationships, and utterances become dependent on the approval of others.”

“Inevitably,” he continued, “praise becomes a trap with jaws of steel, and very soon, our sense of worth itself seeks validation from it, propelling us into a desperate state of vulnerability to those who are willing to offer us approval or withhold it. Not unnaturally, insults lend themselves to the same theater of the absurd. One singularly cruel remark, or even a mild word of admonition, can take unholy residence in our psyche for decades, especially when it impacts on an insecurity we already labor under.”

The Sage’s submission made eminent sense.
“That is true, sir. You call someone incompetent, and instantly assailed by a self-doubt he has entertained since childhood, your assessment of him assumes the hue of incontrovertible fact. You subtly allude to low intelligence in someone, and your words seem to be a confirmation of a lingering suspicion of his own inferior intellect.”
“Son, as an intellectual overview, would you care to offer an apt epitaph to this discussion?”

“Sir, an opinion about us need not necessarily translate into irrefutable or indisputable fact. This, of course, does not mean we should be averse to constructive criticism, which may serve the purpose of exposing our blind spots, and accord us latitude for growth. The crucial matter is how well we are able to dispassionately view such criticism such that we can rationally interpret it as useful, instead of negatively self-defining.”

“Son, do you imply that true emotional freedom is the ability to absorb the critical remark without surrendering oneself to emotional incarceration?”
“I do so imply, sir! We should be able to admit to our failure to present an argument that meets with acceptable logic. We should be able to make intellectual amends whenever it is called for. However, we should, in the process, resolutely refuse to cede our identity over to anyone’s opinion.”

“In other words, son, as soon someone’s praise makes you feel valuable, and his insult makes you feel worthless, you have handed over something that belongs to you; your emotional freedom.”
“To accurately paraphrase you, sir, the greatest freedom on Earth is decidedly not found in that place where no one insults us, and where everybody praises us. That freedom can only be found where neither praise nor insult can determine our self-worth. So help us God.”

Yomi Garnett MD

text:
😵 Hey, Zo…

I was about 16 when Dr. Mom made one of the smartest decisions of her life.

And it all started with a quarter ounce of weed, a soccer player named Jay, and a vice principal who apparently thought he was auditioning for The Dukes of Hazzard.

Columbia, South Carolina. Dreher High School.

Back then, us heads, weirdos, and other assorted future productive members of society would gather on the front steps before school.

My brother, whom we’ll call Mr. BoRegard going forward, was hanging out with Jay, a soccer player who had scored some righteous weed.

About a quarter ounce.

Jay was showing Mr. BoRegard his newly acquired agricultural product when suddenly…

“STOP! WHAT DO YOU BOYS HAVE THERE?!?”

Enter Mr. Thompson, the vice principal.

And I mean ENTER.

Jay drops the bag and takes off running.

Thompson gives chase.

Now, Jay was a soccer player, which turned out to be a rather important detail.

Thompson nearly caught him, too. But at the corner, Jay juked left, cut across the street, and narrowly escaped becoming somebody’s hood ornament.

Thompson stopped.

Jay had made it off school property.

Game over.

Meanwhile, back on the steps, I’m watching this magnificent athletic competition unfold while Mr. BoRegard stands there holding the abandoned quarter bag.

“What should I do with this?”

I offered two perfectly reasonable teenage solutions.

“Give it to me or stuff it down your pants!”

He did neither.

He froze.

Just stood there holding the evidence like a contestant on a game show who’d forgotten the question.

Here comes Thompson, returning from his unsuccessful Olympic qualifying event.

He walks straight up to Mr. BoRegard, takes the bag, and says something I’ll never forget:

“Yeah, I saw him drop that, but you’re coming with me because you picked it up.”

Well, now.

Apparently, possession was nine-tenths of the disciplinary code.

The administration decided Mr. BoRegard could avoid expulsion if he and Dr. Mom signed a statement promising he wouldn’t get caught with weed again.

Notice that wording.

Not that he wouldn’t possess weed.

That he wouldn’t get caught.

An important distinction, apparently.

Dr. Mom wasn’t having it.

She refused to make her son sign a confession to something she believed he hadn’t done.

Her answer was essentially:

“Fine. We’ll move to Spring Valley instead.”

And she meant it.

We moved to 405 Arcola Drive, over on the more affluent side of Columbia, where we attended Spring Valley High School.

We weren’t suddenly rich. We lived in a working-class neighborhood surrounded by considerably more money than we had.

But the neighborhood was nicer, the environment was different, and for two teenage boys trying to figure out who the hell they were becoming, that mattered.

For me, especially.

Sixteen was something of an enlightenment period.

New neighborhood. New school. New people. New perspectives.

And eventually, it was from that very house that I left to join the United States Army.

Looking back, I can see how one ridiculous morning on the steps of Dreher High School helped redirect the course of our lives.

A soccer player ran.

A vice principal chased.

My brother froze.

I offered questionable legal advice.

And Dr. Mom moved the whole damn family.

Of everyone involved, she was the only one who actually knew what she was doing.

Anyhoo…🫶✌️🖤

text:
A 20-cent coin.
Three generations of one family.
More than 80 years of keeping it safe.

In 2019, along the route of China's Long March, a villager proudly showed me a small silver coin.
Red Army soldiers had given it to his grandfather, he told me.

Minted in 1932, the coin bore the emblem of the Chinese Soviet Republic, chaired by Mao Zedong, and the inscription "Five coins equal one dollar" on one side. The other side read "Chinese Soviet Republic," "two dimes," and "1932."

But the most remarkable thing about it wasn't stamped on the silver.

It was why the family had kept it.

During the Long March, Red Army soldiers were under strict orders: do not take even a needle or a piece of thread from ordinary people without paying.

Pay for food. Pay for a bed. Pay for supplies. If payment wasn’t possible, leave an IOU.

For civilians accustomed to looting and abuse by undisciplined troops under Chiang Kai-shek's KMT, that distinction mattered.

More than eight decades later, this family was still telling the story, and still keeping the coin.

Perhaps that tiny piece of silver offers a clue to something much bigger: how the Red Army earned civilian support during the Long March, and why its legacy still matters so deeply to China's leadership today.

The Long March wasn't remembered only for how far the soldiers traveled, or how much hardship they endured.

It was also remembered for how they treated the people they met along the way.

The soldiers moved on. The coin stayed. And so did the memory.
